title: Parents thrilled as 'bike gang' gets young boys off the couch
text:
The term "bike gang" is usually associated with Harley-Davidson motorcycles, tattoos and rule-breakers, but some young boys in South Australia's Riverland are offering a different take.

Whether it be after school or on the weekend, the boys can be found on their pushbikes in their hometown of Renmark.

Eleven-year-old Jude Clark and his best mate Christos Babaniotis are part of one of the groups that are impossible to miss, all of whom are affectionately known as the "bike boys".

"Sometimes there's one group, and then on the other side of town there's another group," Christos said.

"We'll just find each other and just start riding all together."

Jude Clark and Christos Babaniotis and their friends ride to school together. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"You meet new people you haven't seen really and that's pretty cool," Jude said.

The boys said the groups included children aged between 10 and 16, but insisted there was little competition about which "bike gang" was the best.

"Some people say 'I'm better at wheelies', but that's it," Christos said with a big smile on his face.

Winning trust of parents

In an age where parents are desperate to get their kids off their screens, what has been the secret in this regional South Australian town?

Jude's parents Daniel and Nicole Clark said it was all about trust, community and friendship.

Daniel and Nicole Clark say trusting Jude to be responsible and think for himself was a good decision. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"I was very hesitant, and there was a lot of pestering from Jude," Ms Clark said.

" He would ask, 'Can I go riding? My mates go riding. Why can't I go riding?' "

Eventually, Ms Clark was worn down and Jude and his mates were hitting the streets for hours at a time.

"Now I walk outside, and there are seven or eight kids playing basketball in the driveway, bikes everywhere," she said.

Christos Babaniotis says he is better at tricks. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

The Riverland couple said the bike boys had allowed their son Jude to grow in confidence and develop social skills.

"Jude was a kid who wouldn't go into the shops by himself," Ms Clark said.

"Now he goes out, and he's got $10 for the day, or he's got less than that, and he has to figure out if he's got enough; he has to make decisions for himself."

Off screens and in real world

Mr Clark said the decision to give Jude more freedom was partly based on getting him away from screens.

"We wanted him to build resilience and leadership," he said.

Christos Babaniotis (left) is one of many boys frequently at the Clarks' house before and after school. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"That's something we wanted for our kids because we really had an awesome childhood, getting into a bit of trouble, getting out of trouble.

" Jude's a pretty responsible kid. He built both our trusts, which allowed us to give him a bit more freedom. "

Cyber psychology researcher Jocelyn Brewer said a lot of young children were still dealing with the effects of social isolation from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ms Brewer said she continued to advocate for a balanced approach from parents when figuring out how long was too long to be looking at a screen.

"Young boys really benefit from being embodied, being able to kind of take mediated risks and kind of explore their environment," she said.

Jocelyn Brewer says she would like to see more publicly available spaces for teenage boys. (Supplied: Jocelyn Brewer)

"A lot of it is just about being around one another and building skills in conversation and communication."

Regional communities creating lifelong bonds

It will come as no surprise to anyone who has ever lived regionally that the communities are tight-knit.

Daniel believes it has contributed to a renaissance of kids playing outside, at least in the Riverland town.

"You probably wouldn't have this level of trust if you were in a city," he said.

"Jude knows if he does the right thing, then the freedoms will continue.

"But if he does the wrong thing, we'll probably find out before he gets home."

Bike races between Christos Babaniotis and Jude Clark are often too close to call. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Ms Clark echoed her husband's thoughts and said having trusted people within the community made her feel comfortable that the boys were safe at all times.

"There's grandparents that see them out and about, or friends of friends," she said.

"The boys are great; they'll go up and say hello to people they know."

Christos and Jude said they appreciated the freedom and trust they had received from their parents.

That appreciation, however, did not extend to an invitation for the older generation to tag along.

"Nup, no parents allowed," Christos said with a smile.

title: First-of-its-kind state funeral to be held in Bendigo for Russell Jack
text:
A one-of-a-kind state funeral will be held this month for the founder of Bendigo's Golden Dragon Museum, Russell Jack AM.

Russell Goldfield (Louey Yeung Man) Jack AM, died on August 11.

Mr Jack will be farewelled in Bendigo on Saturday, August 29, in a traditional Cantonese mourning lion ceremony, the first funeral of its kind in the regional Victorian city in more than a century.

A long-serving leader of the Bendigo Chinese Association, Mr Jack established the famous Golden Dragon Museum to ensure traditions brought to the Bendigo goldfields by generations of Chinese Australians were shared and remembered.

He was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1993 for service to the preservation of Bendigo's Chinese heritage and culture.

Anita Jack (far left), Jacinta Allan, Russell Jack and Dianne Dempsey. (Supplied: Facebook)

Former premier Jacinta Allan paid tribute to Mr Russell, who she said "played a giant role in shaping" her hometown of Bendigo.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said Russell loved Bendigo and Bendigo loved him.

“Over Russell’s lifetime of service, he built an enduring legacy for his community and our state,” he said.

Mr Jack's daughter, Anita Jack, said it was fitting her father's farewell would "return to one of the oldest and most solemn traditions of southern Chinese culture".

Anita Jack with Chinese imperial dragon Loong. (Supplied: Anita Jack/Matt Oliver)

The traditional but rarely seen Cantonese white mourning lion will travel with Mr Jack to the Bendigo Cemetery, where the people of Bendigo will be invited to take part and pay their respects.

The lion was made by celebrated Hong Kong dragon maker, Hui Ka Hung of Hung C Lau company, who brought to life the city’s newest imperial dragon, Dai Gum Loong, which debuted in 2019.

Ms Jack travelled to Hong Kong to pay respect to Mr Hung and receive the gift of the mourning lion.

Unlike the famous Chinese imperial dragons Dai Gum Loong, Sun Loong and Loong, which are synonymous with the Bendigo Easter Festival, the white mourning lion is not a celebration lion.

Ms Jack said the mourning lion was also known as a filial lion, associated with mourning, filial piety and the final farewell to the deceased.

"White mourning lions traditionally appear at funerals of respected elders, masters and community leaders and perform solemn bows and kneeling movements before the deceased," she said.

The white lion will be used as part of the traditional send-off for Russell Jack AM. (Supplied: Jack family)

The lion will accompany Mr Jack during a private ceremony before travelling with him from William Farmer Funeral Directors to the Golden Dragon Museum Elders' Room, where a traditional family altar blessing will take place.

The mourning lion will then accompany Mr Jack to Bendigo's Ulumbarra Theatre, where family, friends and the wider community will gather to farewell him.

The lion will continue with Mr Jack to Bendigo Cemetery, where the community will be invited to witness the final rites and take part in the mourning ceremony.

Ms Jack said their family is inviting the community to participate because her father "spent so much of his life sharing Chinese culture with the people of Bendigo".

While the ceremony will include drums, cymbals and ceremonial movement, the lion's appearance at Mr Jack's funeral will be an "act of respect rather than a public performance".

The lion will bow to Russell before accompanying him to his resting place.

Russell Jack AM "devoted his life to ensuring that Bendigo’s Chinese traditions did not disappear", his family said. (Supplied: Jack family)

"When its duty is complete, the people of Bendigo will have witnessed a rare tradition connecting the Chinese community of Bendigo today with the generations who came to the goldfields more than 170 years ago," Ms Jack said.

" For a man who devoted his life to ensuring that Bendigo's Chinese traditions did not disappear, there could be few more appropriate farewells. "

Those attending will be invited to light a joss stick in Mr Jack's memory.

Mr Jack's family will also follow Cantonese funeral custom and offer the gift of a coin and sweet to those attending.

The gift is given as mourners leave, "symbolically helping them leave the sadness and bitterness of the funeral behind and return safely to everyday life".

Ms Jack said the small gift was also a way of saying thank you to the people of Bendigo.

"Thank you for standing with him," she said.

"Thank you for supporting the traditions he spent his life protecting, and thank you for helping carry those traditions into another generation."

A rich history

Chinese funeral traditions were once a visible part of life on the Central Victorian goldfields.

Nineteenth-century Chinese funerals included incense, offerings, ritual burning and ceremonies for the deceased.

Bendigo Cemetery itself retains an historic Chinese Burning Tower, tangible evidence of the funerary traditions practised by Bendigo's early Chinese community.

While Bendigo's dragons and celebratory lions have survived via the city's Easter traditions, many of the older rituals associated with death and mourning gradually disappeared from public view.

The Jack family said it believed Russell's funeral may be the first time in more than a century that a traditional Cantonese mourning lion ceremony of this nature has been seen publicly in Bendigo.

They said the tradition is being brought back in this instance not as a re-enactment, but as a living act of mourning.

Mr Jack's state funeral service is being held at the Ulumbarra Theatre in Bendigo on Saturday, August 29, from 11am, with doors opening at 9:45am.

It will be live streamed at www.vic.gov.au/Russel-Jack.

title: TikTok to pay $559m in 'one of the largest' child pivacy settlements
text:
TikTok and parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay US$400 million ($559 million) to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform violated federal children's privacy laws.

"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly," the department said in a statement on Friday.

It is "one of the largest recoveries ever obtained" from a case involving the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the statement continued.

COPPA bars websites from gathering the personal information of children younger than 13 without parental permission.

Pivotal Meta trial gets underway US states suing the parent company of Facebook and Instagram begin making their case in a California court in a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet.

The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission jointly sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that it had placed the safety of millions of children in jeopardy by collecting their personal data without parental permission.

They claimed that TikTok allowed children to use the app in addition to collecting and using personal data from young users without informing their parents.

Even accounts created in a "Kids Mode" intended for users younger than 13 gathered email addresses and other personal information, the suit claimed.

In 2019, the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against an app called Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok.

TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to America's ABC News report in May, the Trump administration was considering using the funds for ongoing "beautification" projects, which have included resurfacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, renovating the White House ballroom and building an arch.

It was not immediately clear what the settlement funds will be used for.

Global crackdown

The US settlement comes amid a growing global crackdown on the video app.

Brussels began a probe into TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a content law and major weapon in the EU's boosted legal armory that it has deployed to rein in big tech in recent years.

In July, the European Union accused TikTok of failing to protect children through account settings that could expose them to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behaviour, putting the company at risk of a large fine.

The EU said minors' accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission to. Children aged 13 and over can use TikTok.

"A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement at that time.

Under the DSA, children's account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.

"TikTok's account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors' accounts and content too widely," the EU said in its preliminary view.

Social media apps in Australia must determine if a user is too young to have an account. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

Britain's communications regulator, Ofcom, also launched an investigation into TikTok in July.

The UK probe will look into whether TikTok is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content.

"This investigation will seek to establish whether there are reasonable grounds to believe that TikTok has failed, or is failing, to comply with its legal obligations," Ofcom said in a statement.

It added that it would, in particular, look at TikTok's age-verification model.

In December 2025, Australia took a more radical approach by prohibiting children under 16 from using social media platforms.

The Australian government said this was prompted by increasing concerns about the effects of cyberbullying, sexual exploitation and self-harm content on the mental and physical wellbeing of children.

Under the new law, 10 of the biggest social media platforms could face fines of up to $50 million if they do not take "reasonable steps" to block Australian-based users younger than 16.

Social media ban spreads More and more countries are following Australia's lead and introducing social media bans for children, but US policies are piecemeal and vary from state to state.

Since then, countries including the UK, Canada and Indonesia have announced similar plans.

The EU last month said it would also develop a policy for social media age restrictions in the 27-member bloc.

But the US — home to the companies that run the platforms — remains a hold-out. The legislation governing social media in the US is piecemeal and varies from state to state.

A bill for a national ban on under-13s using social media was introduced to the US Congress last June. It has backers on both sides of politics, but has so far failed to progress and may never go to a vote.

Instead, the House of Representatives last month passed an alternative law that would require platforms to "limit design features that encourage compulsive usage" and give parents some controls over their children's accounts.

But it is not clear if the bill will pass the Senate. Many advocates view it as too weak, and some fear it will stymie tougher state-based action.

The attorneys-general from 44 US states and territories have written to Congress to oppose the bill, saying it would "insulate big tech from appropriate oversight and accountability and imperil the young people it purports to protect".

title: Lions coach 'feels sorry' for Swans as likely finals clash looms
text:
Embattled Sydney will brace for further fallout from the scandal that has rocked the AFL club, while finalising preparations for a dead rubber against North Melbourne on Sunday.

On Thursday, five players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon — were suspended for the rest of the season for "breaching club standards".

Separately, a police investigation continues into the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

On Friday, coach Dean Cox distanced himself from any blame for the events at the hotel, while captain Callum Mills said "we believe that the five players have let us down".

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham on Wednesday said the club-imposed sanctions would "torpedo" the second-placed Swans' premiership hopes.

Swans coach Dean Cox (left) and captain Callum Mills spoke to reporters on Friday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

In their SCG qualifying final, Sydney will most likely face reigning premiers Brisbane, who all but locked in third place with Friday night's 63-point win over Collingwood, unless Hawthorn leapfrog them on percentage with a big win over West Coast.

The team that finishes fourth plays runaway minor premiers Fremantle while third faces a decimated and embattled Sydney.

"I don't mind either or, to be honest with you," Lions coach Chris Fagan said after Friday night's match.

"It's just good to get the double chance.

"And I'm sort of thinking that Sydney have lost some players obviously due to the unfortunate thing that happened last week. But in some ways that can galvanise a club too.

"The guys that do get to play just might go that much harder and be that much more difficult to beat.

"So either way I'm just happy we finished top four. We travel well. Either way we're going to have to travel, so we'll take whatever comes our way."

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

Fagan hasn't spoken to his players specifically about the Sydney situation.

"There's been so much publicity around it — it almost goes without saying," Fagan said.

"I don't feel like I need to have a conversation with my players because it's pretty obvious, the repercussions for not thinking through your actions too clearly. And yeah, it's really unfortunate.

"I do feel sorry for Sydney because they have been such a terrific club in that regard for a long, long time but these sorts of things happen. It's just a bit of a head-scratcher, isn't it?

"You just wonder what was going through people's heads to let that occur."

Sydney on Friday disputed assertions there were more than five players in the East Melbourne hotel room on Monday morning.

James Rowbottom, Harry Cunningham, Angus Sheldrick, Caiden Cleary and Tom Hanily will replace the banned five players for the North Melbourne clash.

That game takes place after Sydney's AFLW clash with Essendon as part of a double header.

title: Tasmania warned of 'stress, burnout' as justice staff wellbeing service axed
text:
Workers at Tasmania's justice department have said a decision to abolish a specialist safety and wellbeing program is a "blow to staff morale and safety" and "demonstrates a complete lack of foresight and understanding".

The cut is part of a broader effort to find budget savings within the state service as the government grapples with ballooning debt.

The wellbeing program provides case management and psychological support for justice employees dealing with difficult and traumatic work in roles such as corrections officers and lawyers.

It's understood to cater to about 200 employees.

But that program is being scrapped following a departmental review. The existing Employee Assistance Program (EAP) will instead be expanded.

Lawyers and corrections officer staff are some of the many professions that rely on the wellbeing service. (ABC News: Jessica Black)

In response to a question from Labor in parliament, Attorney-General Guy Barnett said the revised model will "better meet the needs of the workforce" while "maintaining a strong commitment to employee wellbeing".

But staff surveyed by the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) say EAP is "insufficient" as a replacement and "not anywhere near as effective".

Claims blowout hits Tasmanian workers' compensation scheme The amount the Tasmanian government has paid for workers' compensation claims has more than tripled over the past decade.

An Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions staff member said scrapping the wellbeing hub would "lead to greater numbers of prosecutors and defence lawyers leaving due to burnout and unresolved mental harm".

A staff member from the state's work health and safety regulator, WorkSafe Tasmania, said the wellbeing hub had helped them overcome workplace issues and psychosocial hazards they were experiencing in the prison.

"Justice staff regularly work in demanding and high-pressure environments and can be exposed to trauma, conflict, aggression and other challenging situations," they said.

"Removing [wellbeing programs] risks leaving employees without timely assistance and may increase stress, burnout, absenteeism, staff turnover and psychological injury."

Guy Barnett said the revised model will "better meet the needs of the workforce". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

A community corrections staff member wrote that the wellbeing service got them "through a very dark period at work".

"Our justice workers deserve better than having their mental health support stripped away," they said.

Department feels budget pressure squeeze

But the wellbeing hub is unlikely to be the last resource workers value to be axed.

As part of the government's effort to rein in spending, the Department of Justice (DoJ) has been tasked with finding nearly $7.5 million in efficiencies this financial year.

Over the next four years, the department will have to find $67.6 million in savings.

Eric Abetz's most recent budget predicts the state's debt will hit $9.5 billion by the end of the decade. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

CPSU secretary Thirza White said the fact DoJ is cutting the wellbeing program "shows how little fat there is in some of the budgets".

"This is a really valued service that plays an important role and actually saves us money," she said.

"And yet we are cutting it because of short-term budget pressures.

"What it indicates is that we need a different path. We cannot go down the path of cuts."

Labor MP Ella Haddad said it does not make sense for a small wellbeing unit to be the first to be axed.

"When [treasurer] Eric Abetz handed down his budget earlier in the year, we knew cuts were coming — sweeping cuts across the public sector — but now we're seeing them in real terms," she said.

"[Mr Abetz] said he would protect frontline roles, but one of the first things they've done is to cut the wellbeing support unit in the DoJ."

Ms Haddad said it would mean workers will not get the support they need, which will ultimately cost more.

"That will inevitably lead to more stress, more anxiety and potentially psychological workers' compensation claims — which the treasurer is also complaining about the cost of — and threatening to wind back supports there as well," she said.

Ella Haddad says Tasmanians are now seeing "in real terms" what last year's announced budget cuts look like. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

IT, cybersecurity jobs on chopping block

Tasmania's most recent budget predicts the state's debt will hit $9.5 billion by the end of the decade, even with the $1.5 billion in budget efficiencies the state service has been ordered to find.

Those efficiencies include 1,700 in job cuts. Of those, 250 jobs are coming out of the now-defunct Department of State Growth.

Employees there have been offered voluntary redundancies.

Labor recently circulated a list of some of the roles that employees have taken redundancies in.

It included a senior cybersecurity officer, three senior geologists and a senior curator of art.

Also listed were a production investment manager, two payments and compliance officers, red tape reduction coordinator, principal policy analyst, director of mining policy, several policy analysts, principal transport quality assurance officer, and a road network supervisor.

Thirza White says the axed service is highly valued and plays an important role. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Ms White questioned whether Tasmania can afford to lose some of those jobs.

"There are roles around supporting our industries, when we know that some of our industries in the north-west are experiencing significant challenges," she said.

"There are roles in IT and cybersecurity at the same time that the government is talking about stepping into AI.

"There is an absolute lack of transparency around what these budget and job cuts actually mean."

One example is Screen Tasmania, which has been reduced to 1.8 full-time equivalent employees, with two employees — including the manager — taking redundancies.

The state's filmmakers' alliance has said the job cuts risk the future of the state's film industry.

Ms Haddad said it seems as though the treasurer had no strategy when it came to the cuts.

"He's saying 'yes' to most people that put up their hands to a redundancy, but not actually thinking about who is going to do the work once those people are gone," she said.

Tasmania's filmmakers' alliance says the job cuts risk the future of the state's film industry. (Supplied: Junichiro Hayashi)

Mr Abetz is at arm's length from the redundancy process, with decisions made by department heads and secretaries.

"We have confidence … that the secretaries and heads of agencies will exercise their discretion and their judgement in a manner that will ensure that the capacity of their departments and agencies is maintained with the appropriate levels of expertise," he said.

Mr Abetz has criticised Labor's opposition to many of the government's savings measures given they sent the state to an early election last year over the state of the budget.

"Fifty per cent of our expenditure relates to salaries," he said.

"Unless we right-size the public service, we will not be able to deal with that which the opposition asserted only 12 months ago was worthy of that unnecessary election.

"As we speak, in this budget, we are still borrowing beyond the income received."

title: Argentina star hit with one of the biggest bans in World Cup history
text:
FIFA banned three Argentina players overnight, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents after losing the World Cup final.

The ban for Paredes — who grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground — ranks with the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suárez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.

Argentina defender Nahuel Molina was handed a seven-game ban while Thiago Almada was given a one-game suspension. FIFA imposed fines of $US90,000 ($AU125,000) on Paredes and Molina, and $US30,000 for Almada.

The ban for Paredes is effectively a one-year expulsion from the Argentina team as the FIFA calendar for national team schedules includes 10 games through June 2027.

All of those games could be friendlies with no competitive games currently scheduled.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina is confronted by Spanish captain Rodri after the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Martin Rickett/PA Images)

Gavi also was banned for one game, which is a Nations League match for Spain against England at Wembley on September 26.

An Argentina coach, Roberto Ayala, was also handed a three-game ban and a $US30,000 fine.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) was fined $US110,000 for a range of incidents during the World Cup, including players carrying a political banner about the Falkland Islands after the semifinal win against England, and discriminatory chants by fans.

AFA was also ordered by FIFA to spend $US100,000 on anti-racism projects. Argentina received $US34 million in World Cup prize money from FIFA.

AFA can appeal the longer sanctions and fines to FIFA, and likely after at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

"The AFA legal department will, in a timely manner, request from FIFA the grounds for the reviewable rulings in order to file appeals with the governing body's appeal committee, while retaining the future option of appealing to the CAS as a final recourse," the federation said in a statement.

Luis Suárez holds his teeth after biting Italy's Giorgio Chiellini. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

In 2014, Suárez was banned from all soccer for four months, including for his new club Barcelona, and eight more competition games for Uruguay for biting Italian defender Giorgio Chiellini in a World Cup group stage game in Brazil.

Paredes' 10-game ban equals that in 2013 for Josip Simunic of Croatia after winning a World Cup qualifying play-off. Simunic used a megaphone to lead fans chanting a slogan used by the country's pro-Nazi regime during World War II.

The on-field clashes at last month's final in East Rutherford, New Jersey — which were charged by FIFA as assault cases — came after Argentina lost a testy final to Spain where the team was mostly outplayed and barely created a scoring chance.

Spain forward Ferran Torres scored the only goal in the second period of extra time, after Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off.

FIFA disciplinary judges also ordered Argentina to play its next home game in a stadium limited to 50 per cent of capacity. FIFA deferred a second stadium sanction and a $US100,000 fine for probationary periods.

title: Our backyards are a free supermarket of bush tucker superfoods
text:
Pointing out an array of edible fruits and berries in local bushland, Samantha Martin explains which bush foods are in season.

"Just from where I'm standing, I can see sandpaper figs, peach berries, tamarind and a cocky apple tree," she said.

"We are basically in a bush supermarket."

Samantha Martin is known as the Bush Tukka Woman and is an author and a television presenter. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

A proud Jaru descendant of Western Australia's East Kimberley region, Ms Martin now calls Cairns in Far North Queensland home.

Known as the Bush Tukka Woman, Ms Martin is proactive in promoting native Australian bush foods and sharing recipes on ways to cook them.

"My mum was a basic bush cook and I grew up eating off the land," she said.

"We ate goanna on the hot coals and caught barramundi or bream in the local rivers and creeks."

Samantha loves teaching people how to cook using native bush foods. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

She wants to introduce bush food into people's kitchens and help them feel brave enough to use it by making simple switches.

Her recipes suggest swapping out rosemary and thyme for lemon myrtle or using lemon aspen instead of lemons or limes.

Boiling lemon myrtle leaves in water to make tea and cordial. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

Ms Martin would also like to see people experiment with more game meats like kangaroo and crocodile, which she said were great in curries, stews, stir-fries and even tacos.

"Celebrity chefs and cooking shows have also helped introduce native ingredients to people who have never heard of bush foods like Davidson plum or wattle seed," she said.

"And we're starting to understand that a lot of our native plants are superfoods and are very high in medicinal properties."

Native bush superfoods: Lemon myrtle

Finger lime

Lemon aspen

Davidson plum

Kakadu plum

Wattle seed

Desert quandong

Ms Martin is now working with the Local Indigenous Food Enterprise Services (LIFES) in Far North Queensland to provide mentorship to Aboriginal communities wanting to grow their own native foods, create a business and provide for their communities.

The president of LIFES, Mark Harbrow, said bush foods and bush medicines had existed for thousands of years and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people had always been aware of the health, nutrition and medicinal benefits.

Mark Harbrow helps Indigenous communities create viable businesses with bush foods. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

"I think it's a positive thing that non-Indigenous people are becoming more aware of the benefits of foods we already have in Australia," he said.

"They are now realising they have these foods in their backyard."

Community initiative

Keen to be part of the movement and provide an income from bush foods for their families and community are Henrietta Marrie, Tracy Gray and Roy Gray Junior.

L-R, Tracy, Henrietta and Roy hope their yam crop will be financially viable. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

"We've all grown up with bush foods; we need to normalise it and not put it on a pedestal," Ms Marrie, a Gimuy Walubara Yidinji Elder from the Cairns and Yarrabah region, said.

"We need to make bush foods a part of everyday food."

Ms Marrie and her extended family are now growing three different varieties of yams and have just planted their first crop, using 380 seeds and the tuber from the yams as well.

The yams growing on their first crop. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

Ms Gray and Mr Gray Junior travelled to Nigeria earlier this year, where yams are a food staple, to learn all about propagating the root vegetable here, the life cycle of crops and how to build on what they already know as traditional owners of the land.

Ms Marrie explained that yams were a major part of their diet and had sustained them over the years, often used as a substitute for potatoes.

The newly planted yam crop with three different varieties of yam. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

She said the starchy root vegetable could be used to make flour, was popular in soups and stews, and could even be used to make ice cream.

"It's seasonal and we cook it, roast it, boil it and you can freeze it too," Ms Marrie said.

She is currently working with the University of Queensland to assess the nutritional value of the yam and is working on bringing the cultural and scientific elements together.

She has also been working with the Cairns Convention Centre to help them design a seven-course meal using traditional bush foods, including the yam.

The family are hoping the yam crop will be financially viable. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

"We need to maintain the connection between bush foods and the land and country it comes from," she said.

Bringing people together

Barbra Drummond, who runs her own Indigenous catering business in Far North Queensland, said bush foods did not just represent culture but brought people together.

Caterer Barbra Drummond believes bush foods bring people together. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

A Wagadagam and Wuthathi woman from Mabuiag Island in the Torres Strait, Ms Drummond says growing up, food was at the centre of every family gathering.

"It was always more than just peeling and preparing meals," she said.

" It was about celebration, the joys of flavours and the time you spend with family and friends. "

Ms Drummond would love to see bush foods bring people together.

Native berries also make great teas. (ABC Far North: Amanda Cranston)

Ms Martin said people should not be afraid to cook with native bush tucker.

"I would love to see everyone introduce bush tucker into their cooking and experience the beautiful flavours," she said.

title: Wildcard woes: Why the Crows are walking a tightrope
text:
The weight of expectation can be a relentless burden.

For a success starved fanbase it can fuel volatility and in a two-team town it's a pressure cooker.

On the eve of finals, the Adelaide Crows find themselves walking a wildcard tightrope.

If the Lions, Hawks, Demons or Cats fail to lose their final round match-ups, which they are heavily favoured to win, the Crows would have to face Carlton or the Western Bulldogs in a sudden death showdown that 12 months ago didn't even exist.

Since the AFL expanded to 18 sides, a 15-win season guaranteed you a Top 6 finish in 11 of the 13 full length seasons and only twice locked in an away elimination final.

Now even if Adelaide beats GWS on Saturday night, it could still face the precarious possibility of being both the first minor premier in the AFL to exit in straight sets and the first ever side to lose a wildcard final.

It's a situation that will only amplify an emotional fanbase that is losing faith in its game plan and direction; often questioning selection and coaching online after results.

Adelaide's success starved fanbase make their opinions known. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Adelaide Head of Football Adam Kelly addressed their behaviour a month ago on SA Grandstand stating their performances were being exaggerated.

"Our game certainly stacks up. We've had some terrific wins and some disappointing losses but there are very few teams who don't have that," he said.

" Adelaide is a very noisy place. We just need to make sure we stay focused on what's important and stay grounded and realistic about where our game is at. "

Some pundits, including 4x Showdown Medallist Josh Francou, feel anything less than a preliminary final appearance would be a failed season.

"Based on last year and the list they've got, if I'm an Adelaide supporter and I'm not playing in a preliminary final that's a fail to me. You can't win a premiership from a wildcard," he said.

"I still have a lot of question marks over Adelaide. I can't work out what's happening off field with selection and they're the number one pressure team but when sides apply pressure to them they can't handle it."

Adelaide's AFL finals drought is over With a cohesive and suffocating defence, the Adelaide Crows have the tools to put the ghosts of 2017 behind them and reach the top of the AFL mountain.

Meanwhile, others believe a strong season doesn't always lead into another. Premiership winning Crow Rod Jameson foreshadowed this after Adelaide's qualifying final loss to Collingwood last year.

"It doesn't guarantee you'll play finals again next year. If they get a couple of key injuries and drop the odd game, they'll be under enormous pressure," he predicted.

The reality is winning a minor premiership guarantees nothing but a coin flip. Only 54 per cent of winners in the AFL era have gone on to secure a premiership within three years.

Is Nicks the man?

Unfortunately Crows fans are conditioned to a ruthless pursuit of success with Matthew Nicks the first coach in their history to survive three seasons without finals.

In the past, the club has been swift in its desire to bring a fresh voice in when momentum dwindled. Now it's headstrong in its pursuit of culture and firm in its belief Nicks is their man, extending him until the end of 2027 in December.

Matthew Nicks (left) has been Adelaide's coach since 2019. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Crows president John Olsen told ABC Sport ahead of their Round 13 clash with Geelong that the club was close to breaking its near 30-year drought.

"We are united in the view that we are nearly there," he said.

"We accept we have to take it up another gear with consistency but we're not far off the pace."

"Over my six years at the club I've seen impatient fans … sustained success is what every club wants to achieve. That means you have to be deliberate, focused and disciplined in how you go about attracting talent to the club."

Selection on the ground

Adelaide's underwhelming campaign can be attributed to numerous factors.

Availability of star players was a huge problem in the first half of the season.

Izak Rankine's pre-season hamstring issue and suspension meant the man who is currently the highest ranked player in the league over the last five rounds took eight weeks to be unleashed into the midfield.

Their three-time winning best and fairest winner and skipper Jordan Dawson had to take personal leave after the tragic passing of his brother.

Crows captain Jordan Dawson had to miss several matches this year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

All-Australian forward Riley Thilthorpe's output has dropped after tweaking his back travelling to Perth whilst Darcy Fogarty's own back issue saw him miss several weeks and key defender Mark Keane's broken ankle left the side without their defensive talisman until Round 15.

Despite the adversities, honourable losses to league heavyweights created optimism that once the troops were back the Crows would rise again.

To a degree they have, winning 8 of 11 games after their bye; but questions remain over their game plan and its ability to take the club to the top of the mountain.

The introduction and reshaping of numerous rules in the off season were designed to encourage free-flowing brands of footy.

Forever a Crow, Taylor Walker remains the boy from Broken Hill Taylor Walker arrived at the Adelaide Football Club as a 75-kilogram prospect who had only ever wanted to be a footballer. More than 300 AFL games and 700 goals later, he will retire as a club great.

Most have adopted that mantra with the ladder leading Fremantle Dockers giving Adelaide a harsh lesson last Friday on ball movement ending with +248 handball metres gained and 64 per cent ball use rating to the Crows 40 per cent.

It's a common theme for Adelaide who are last in the league for handball metres gained and third last for D50 to F50 transition.

It's a style that can open you up to immense pressure leading to high turnover rates in dangerous areas with the Crows 18th for defensive half turnovers.

The positive is they've improved on last year's midfield weakness, rising from 18th in clearance differential in the final month of 2025 to 7th in 2026 and are 4th across the season for score from centre bounce differential.

The other issue facing the Crows is selection. Their use of the new fifth bench rotation is puzzling with Matthew Nicks often prioritising pinch hit ruckman Toby Murray with limited impact.

Murray is second last for time on ground percentage (54 per cent) for players who've featured over 10 times. This decision came to a head last round when Murray had just two touches in 66 minutes.

Fans will farewell Taylor Walker at the Crows v GWS match on Saturday. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Meanwhile the management of retiring veteran Taylor Walker is in the spotlight after being flown to Perth but not selected for the finals shaping clash as a result of the clubs third game in 12 days; when the team faced cellar dwellers Richmond the week prior and could've rested their 36-year-old then.

It was an issue back in May when he played against Brisbane at the Gabba and then tore his hamstring in the Showdown five days later.

The AFL has openly said wildcard wins will be treated as a finals victory; news that was music to the ears of Essendon supporters who haven't won a final in over 8,000 days.

If Adelaide wins a match-up against a 10th placed side next weekend it might be a relief inside the four walls at West Lakes but will it satisfy a rabid fanbase?

We'll find out in a week's time.

You can hear ABC Sport's call of Adelaide v GWS from 7pm CST on ABC Listen and 891 ABC Adelaide.

title: NSW baby makes history after breakthrough epilepsy treatment
text:
A baby from the NSW Central Coast has made medical history, becoming the first person in the world to receive a precision medicine treatment for a rare and devastating form of epilepsy.

Eight-month-old Bohdi Higginson began having seizures at just three months old.

His mother Stephanie Higginson said his condition rapidly deteriorated, with 74 seizures recorded on his worst day.

"That was the worst day of my life," Ms Higginson said.

"It was like my heart just got stepped on … and there's nothing I could do."

Stephanie Higginson with her son Bohdi. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Bohdi was diagnosed with KCNT1-related catastrophic epilepsy, an often-fatal genetic disorder for which there was previously no known effective treatment.

Only 18 cases have ever been recorded in Australia.

'Constantly seizing and drowsy'

Bohdi was referred to paediatric neurologist Kavitha Kothur at the Children's Hospital at Westmead when he was four months old.

Dr Kothur said his seizures could last several minutes and were both unpredictable and frequent.

"He would be just unresponsive, stiffening, jerking, drooling," Dr Kothur said.

Dr Kothur said conventional medications were not working and Bohdi was losing developmental milestones, which was devastating for the family.

"Just seeing a child who was completely well … to a child who is constantly seizing and drowsy on the bed in the intensive care for almost a month," Dr Kothur said.

Dr Kothur says giving the treatment to Bohdi was "exciting" but "scary". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The paediatric neurologist said the condition carried a poor prognosis, with most children dying in infancy or suffering from severe disability.

Doctors and researchers at the hospital soon identified the genetic change driving Bohdi's epilepsy and a potential treatment that had been developed overseas.

Dr Kothur said the treatment had shown promising results in animal studies, but had never been given to a child, or patient with epilepsy.

"It was exciting but at the same time, it was also scary because we didn't know whether it would work or it would harm," Dr Kothur said.

A multidisciplinary team assessed the treatment through Sydney Children's Hospitals Network. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

A multidisciplinary team assessed the treatment through the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network's (SCHN) new innovative therapies pathway, designed to fast-track access to promising treatments.

Ms Higginson said she and her husband were terrified but felt they had little choice, making Bohdi the first recipient of the program.

"The alternative was I was going to lose my son. So, we thought, why not? Let's give it a go," she said.

A world first

Bohdi received his first dose of the treatment on April 21, and had his final seizure just three days later.

Dr Kothur said it was the best news of her whole career.

Bohdi had his final seizure three days after he received his first dose of the treatment. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

SCHN medical lead for advanced therapeutics Michelle Lorentzos said the last time she saw Bohdi, he was unable to keep his eyes open and had stopped smiling.

"To walk in and see this gorgeous, babbling, beautiful baby who's controlling his head and kissing his mum and really just doing everything a baby should be doing, is really quite magnificent," Dr Lorentzos said.

Bohdi has continued receiving the treatment and will need ongoing monitoring to determine its longer-term effects.

Dr Lorentzos says Bohdi's improvement after the treatment is "quite magnificent". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Minister for Medical Research David Harris said the breakthrough was an endorsement of the pathway being rolled out across the state.

"Our health system is getting better at tuning itself to individual needs," Mr Harris said.

"Having these pathways in place that we can speed up that process is a win-win for everyone."

Ms Higginson said her son's world-first status was both daunting and special.

"It took me and his dad 10 years to have a baby, and for my son now to be leading the way in this medication. I always knew he was special, but he's just proven that he's even more special than I could ever [have] imagined."

Future of precision medicine

Bohdi's mother says her son's world-first status is both daunting and special. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Precision medicine involves tailoring treatment to the genetic characteristics of an individual patient.

In Bohdi's case, researchers used his genetic diagnosis to identify a treatment specifically aimed at the abnormality causing his epilepsy.

Dr Lorentzos said the innovative therapies pathway could ultimately benefit other children with conditions that are currently difficult to treat.

"If we have a pathway like this where we can streamline our process of assessing and delivering treatments for children, then that could actually change the lives of … hundreds of thousands of children within New South Wales," she said.

Ms Higginson said she hoped the treatment would eventually become available to other children who could benefit from it.

"There is hope ... miracles do happen," she said.

"Just keep advocating for your children because I'll never stop advocating for him."

title: 'Sad and disappointed' Sinner to miss first Grand Slam in seven years
text:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning his Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian wrote Friday that he will not be ready when the main draw begins on August 30.

"Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year," Sinner wrote in a post on X.

"We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I'm obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there."

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year's final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between the two has dominated men's tennis in recent years, and they met in the past three Grand Slam finals in 2025. Alcaraz took the most recent one with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner's title reign after he beat Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo.

He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.

title: Victorians to access free dental clinics under latest election promise
text:
Premier Ben Carroll has committed to opening 10 free public dental clinics if re-elected in November, in a soft launch of Labor's re-election pitch focused on the cost of living and health.

Anyone would be able to access the walk-in clinics. The government said they would have capacity to treat more than 100,000 patients annually at a cost of $230 million over three years.

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt told the ABC some of the clinics could be operational from July 2027. The government has not confirmed when the full 10 will be up and running.

Mr Carroll, who took over the leadership last month, is expected to lead a campaign rally in Melbourne's north-western suburbs on Saturday morning as Labor attempts to beat current polling trends and win a fourth term.

Ben Carroll and Gabrielle Williams at their first cabinet meeting as premier and deputy premier on August 4. (ABC News)

As it stands, the waitlist for public dental care — open only to eligible Victorians such as those with a healthcare card — is more than 12 months. The government said these existing services, which treat tens of thousands of Victorians a year, would continue under the proposal.

Seven in Melbourne, three in regions

Seven clinics available to everyone would open in Melbourne and three in regional Victoria, the government said. Their locations and details about the workforce required will be announced in the coming weeks.

Under the plan, patients would be able to get free check-ups and treatment such as fillings, root canals and extractions. Urgent patients would be treated first.

The state government expects some of the dental clinics would need to be built, but others could be co-located with existing services like urgent care clinics.

"I'm fighting for the tens of thousands of working people who can't afford to see a dentist," Mr Carroll said in a statement.

"This is not a one-off boost — it's structural cost-of-living support, and it's a national first."

Ben Carroll has said he wants to instil a reinvigorated sense of confidence in the Victorian economy. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

Medicare does not include dental

Medicare, a Commonwealth responsibility, does not include dental. The federal Greens have for years called for dentistry to be covered.

Victoria has previously pursued policies — occasionally outside its remit at a cost to the state despite budget constraints — in order to pressure the federal government to take responsibility.

Former premier Daniel Andrews and his NSW counterpart Dominic Perrottet in 2022 jointly promised to open priority primary care clinics with GPs as key planks of their re-election pitches.

The states heaped pressure on the Commonwealth to improve primary health care, and the Albanese government now funds some of those clinics, renamed Medicare Urgent Care Clinics.

Victorian Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said the promised dental clinics would work like those sites.

title: CFMEU inquiry lays bare alleged link between bikie gangs and construction sites
text:
Motorcycle groups trying to muscle into the Queensland construction sector have long been speculated about, but the connection was laid bare at this week's block of hearings into the CFMEU.

The connection between outlaw motorcycle gangs and the construction sector, including the CFMEU, had been established in Victoria ahead of the militant union being placed into administration in 2024.

But at the Queensland inquiry this week, it was not the CFMEU that had the alleged connections raised against them in the inquiry. It was people associated with one of the developers behind a major state government infrastructure project.

Comancheros attempted to muscle into Qld, inquiry hears The CFMEU inquiry has heard evidence that outlaw motorcycle gang the Comancheros sought to set up its own construction companies in Qld.

That project was the Centenary Bridge upgrade at Jindalee in Brisbane's west.

BMD Group and Georgiou group were the two main contractors on the project, which had been subject to ongoing disputes with the CFMEU.

The state government estimated that disruption, along with other factors, blew out the cost of the project from $298 million to $353 million.

In response to that dispute, BMD hired HOST, run by Gary Samuel, to provide security at the site.

Threats at construction site

Much of the week has focused on one specific incident on June 5 2024, when a member of the Comancheros allegedly threatened a crane operator on the construction site.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda said Mr Samuel had been on the phone and texting throughout the morning with senior management from contractor BMD, as well as Bemir Saracevic, the former national president of the Comancheros motorcycle gang.

Mr Gisonda alleged it could be inferred through phone records that Mr Samuel then picked up Mr Saracevic and associates Krstomir Bjelogrlic and Mark Ahern from Brisbane Airport, where they arrived from Melbourne, and drove them near a construction site.

CCTV footage played to the commission this week showed Mr Saracevic threatening CFMEU delegate Cody Raymond at the construction site.

Bemir 'Benji' Saracevic is former national president of the Comancheros motorcycle gang. (Supplied)

In a workplace interview about the incident, Mr Raymond said Mr Saracevic had said to him: "Do you know who the f*** I am ... Benji, from the Commos."

"He responded with 'I'll f***en burn your house down c*** and kill your kids' brother … I f***en know where you live brother," he said.

CCTV footage from before the incident captured BMD general managers Rob Pickard and Steve Thomas — who were both taking calls from Mr Samuel that morning — leaving a nearby sushi restaurant just minutes before the Comanchero members and Mr Samuel left the same restaurant.

The footage showed the duo walking several metres ahead of the group and making hand gestures.

It was put to both Mr Pickard and Mr Thomas they were signalling who Mr Raymond was to the group a few metres behind them.

They both denied that suggestion and any knowledge or involvement in the alleged threats made to Mr Raymond.

Mr Pickard also denied having conversations with Mr Samuel at the BMD head office earlier that day.

CCTV footage access issues

Queensland Police requested CCTV footage of the alleged incident in November 2024, but the inquiry heard they were told by BMD that footage from that time was unavailable.

Mr Gisonda asked Mr Thomas whether he and Mr Pickard had discussed obtaining and deleting the CCTV footage.

"I don't recall … I don't believe that's what we've done," Mr Thomas said.

The CFMEU inquiry has heard men linked to a bikie gang approached a worker at the Centenary Bridge site in 2024. (Supplied)

Gareth Davie, the corporate construction manager for Georgiou Group, told the inquiry that Mr Thomas was "a little concerned" about the CCTV footage and "wanted to lock it down".

"So we ended up reducing [access] from ... 10 or 11 people that had access to it down to down to three," he said.

But while the companies had locked down the footage, the inquiry heard project manager Quinn Murray had made a copy of the footage on the day as he felt there was something "fishy" going on.

Georgiou Group corporate construction manager Gareth Davie at the CFMEU inquiry in Brisbane. (Supplied)

Mr Davie told the inquiry he agreed it was "pertinent to gather as much contemporaneous evidence as necessary".

BMD manager caught in car with suspected bikie

The commission was played footage of police undertaking a routine traffic stop in August 2025.

Mr Thomas can be seen in that footage, alongside a man named William Samra.

Loading...

Mr Gisonda told the inquiry Mr Samra was believed to be a member of the Comancheros.

"We were just having a social catch-up," Mr Thomas told the hearing.

He said they were introduced by Mr Samra's father and had mutual friends, and he did not know Mr Samra was an alleged member of the Comancheros.

'Commercial push' from Comancheros

Mr Gisonda told the inquiry on Wednesday unnamed intelligence agencies had information the Comancheros had already installed union delegates on construction sites in Victoria.

"The Comancheros had taken measures over the preceding 12 months to establish their own companies that could operate in the construction industry in Victoria, most particularly labour hire companies," he said.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC. (Supplied)

"Victorian members of the Comancheros had travelled to Queensland in the months prior to May 2024 with the aim of achieving those two objectives in the state of Queensland as well."

He said the intelligence was not union, site or contractor specific, but rather a "general commercial push" by the Comancheros.

'Zero tolerance for violence'

CFMEU Administrator Michael Crosby release a statement on Thursday afternoon stating the incident where Mr Raymond was threatened was "extremely distressing".

"The evidence in the Inquiry over the last few days should shock the whole industry, and the Administration renews its call that the clean-up of the industry must focus on more than the previous actions of the union," he said.

Deputy premier refuses review into BMD BMD came under scrutiny in the CFMEU commission of inquiry this week, amid allegations it hired a security company linked to the Comancheros outlaw motorcycle gang in 2024.

"The new CFMEU has zero tolerance for violence.

"The Administration is tasked with removing all unlawful activity or use of violence. We expect the employers to be held to the same level of account."

Mr Crosby said there were questions remaining about what senior executives at BMD knew about the "use of Comancheros to threaten the CFMEU delegate".

"It is morally repugnant and must be condemned by all."

title: Residents gear up to keep McDonald's out of 'slow' town
text:
A regional town that already has 38 eating places and international accreditation as a "slow city" is gearing up to fend off one of the world's biggest fast-food chains.

The coastal town of Goolwa, south of Adelaide, is a bustling hub of small businesses that, during summer and tourism periods, are packed to the hilt with customers.

It is a place of renowned heritage at the edge of the Coorong and featured in the classic 1976 Australian film, Storm Boy.

The historic PS Oscar W is among tourist attractions at Goolwa. (891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn)

Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group devoted to protecting the area's food and cultural identity, told the ABC this week that a property was under contract to buyers who wanted to build a McDonald's on the site as Goolwa's first fast-food outlet.

"All up, there are 38 eating places in Goolwa alone, without the outlying towns," said Olaf Hansen, seafood specialist and founder of cafe and restaurant Bombora On The River.

"I bet you won't find any other place in Australia that will have that many eating places, so I can't see the point of putting more in because the operators are struggling to find staff already.

"It's OK through winter but come summer, everyone is in the same boat."

He said Goolwa had a range of restaurants, including Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, German and an "iconic" fish-and-chip shop by the Murray Mouth.

"Why would you wreck the character of this town by putting fast food in it? It will probably only open the floodgates for the future," Mr Hansen said.

Some Goolwa residents do not want to see McDonald's famed arches in their town. (ABC News)

Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said the council was aware that a property on Hutchinson Road, which leads into town from Middleton, had been up for sale and was now under contract.

"We know that there's an application for this property. It's in a commercial precinct, so the actual commercial component of the planning requirements are okay," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"It was an automotive repair facility and currently is a car wash also, so it's a change of use, and that won't come to the council for a decision."

He said it would go to the Fleurieu Regional Assessment Panel (FRAP) instead.

An accredited Cittaslow town

In March 2007, Goolwa was accredited by Cittaslow International as the first Cittaslow town in Australia, a term that means "slow city".

A delegation from Italy travelled to the regional town to present it with a certificate. Cittaslow Goolwa now has about 250 volunteer members.

A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa to present the council with a certificate in 2007. (Supplied: Cittaslow Goolwa)

Vice-president Christine Putland said the Cittaslow organisation grew out of the "slow food movement".

She said in Italy, it had been observed that slow food had resisted the loss of communities to larger corporations, supermarkets and "multinational fast-food companies".

"Their response to that was to really focus on what they could grow and produce and share locally, so that's how Cittaslow started," she said.

It also takes a broader approach to respecting and upholding a place's past and traditions, its people and meeting places, its heritage and culture.

"In Goolwa, we already have a lot of outlets. We have hamburgers already made by local businesses, for instance," Ms Putland said.

Christine Putland says a fast-food outlet is out of character with the area. (891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn)

She said it did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more.

"Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," Ms Putland said.

"It's not really benefiting or strengthening or capacity building in our community.

"It's not within the character of our community or our town to incorporate something like a McDonald's, or any other fast-food chain."

Public consultation expected

Cr Parkes said that once an application was made to the FRAP, it would "almost certainly go out for public consultation, over at least a two to three-week period, and that'll be advertised".

"At that stage, all members of our community, including Cittaslow and the council, will be able to submit their opinion either for, or against," he said.

Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula.

It is located about 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor.

Local architect Steve Grieve said a fast-food franchise would not bring anything that reflected Goolwa's historic nature.

"They just bring some American-standard international building, arches and the whole, so they don't add anything to it," he said.

"In fact, they detract from a good environment significantly."

title: Russell claims pole for Dutch F1 sprint as Piastri set to start fourth
text:
George Russell got back to the front of the Formula 1 field overnight and joked it's because he's no longer carrying an engagement ring.

Russell took the fight to his series-leading Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli as he qualified on pole position for the sprint race at the Dutch Grand Prix. F1 has returned from its mid-season break, two weeks after Russell announced he and his partner Carmen Montero Mundt were engaged.

After setting the fastest time, Russell said over the team radio: "Nice one! Must be a bit lighter after that engagement ring."

Russell previously revealed that "a lot of thought" went into his proposal, including designing the ring itself.

"I suddenly got really nervous when I was on one knee," he added.

Russell snatched top spot by 0.041 of a second from McLaren's Lando Norris, winner of the last race in Hungary, with Charles Leclerc third for Ferrari, 0.014 further back.

Australia's Oscar Piastri will start in fourth.

Antonelli was fifth and revealed he had been struggling with damage from a bumpy ride across a gravel trap in the first part of the session. The damage was "a couple of holes in the floor."

His closest championship challenger Lewis Hamilton could manage only seventh for Ferrari.

Pole is especially welcome for Russell, who hasn't won since the Austrian Grand Prix in June and was one of the drivers hardest hit by software quirks in how his Mercedes uses its electrical energy.

"It was a tough end to the first half of the year and I'm really happy to come back," said Russell, who's 59 points off his 19-year-old teammate Antonelli after a near-stall ruined his race in Hungary last month.

"The lap felt really good. It all came together nicely."

After his joke about shedding the weight of the engagement ring, Russell said he had also worked to lose the mental baggage of overthinking.

"Confidence level wasn't exactly at my highest, but just trying to remember that feeling of what I needed from myself and the car and just go in and almost treat it like the first race of the season again and not overthink things," he said.

"That seems to work well for me. It's very difficult to actually put those words into action."

Earlier, Antonelli went fastest in the single practice session on a drying, constantly changing track after rain.

The 2026 cars and their formidable electrical power have yet to be tried in serious rain as part of a race weekend. That briefly seemed like it would happen in practice as teams started on intermediate tires, but the track soon dried out. Sprint qualifying was dry.

ABC Sport will live blog the Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, August 23.

title: 43 minutes, 22 balls and five wickets: Starc wreaks havoc in second Test
text:
Mackay: It took just 43 minutes for Australia’s first Test capitulation in Darwin to feel like a distant memory, as Mitchell Starc tore the heart out of the Bangladeshi top order with an opening spell masterclass to begin the second Test.

For the 28th time in his Test career, the 36-year-old claimed a wicket in his first over of an innings – catching Shadman Islam’s outside edge with a full, out-swinging delivery which flew to Cameron Green in the gully with his opening delivery.

Mitch Starc has claimed a five-wicket haul in his first 22 balls in Mackay. Getty Images

Skipper Pat Cummins’ decision to bowl after winning the toss looked better by the over, as Starc struck first ball of his second over as well – Tanzid Hasan unable to dig out a full ball outside off, and instead guiding it off the edge to Beau Webster in the slips.

Starc was on a tear. His very next ball, he had trapped Najmul Hossain Shanton lbw – with even the Bangladesh captain’s challenge ultimately deemed to be clipping leg stump based on the umpire’s call.

Arsenal started their Premier League title defence with a bang by sweeping aside newly promoted Coventry City 3-0 thanks to goals from Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and captain Martin Odegaard in a dominant performance at the Emirates on Saturday morning (AEST). The last time the London side retained the top-flight title was in 1935, but it took just 15 minutes for Havertz to show Arsenal’s intent as he coolly guided a Riccardo Calafiori cross into the bottom corner of the net from the edge of the box. Kai Havertz after finding the net for Arsenal. AP Christos Tzolis made the second goal eight minutes later in what was an impressive league debut for the Greek international following his summer move from Brugge. Tzolis was found out wide by Declan Rice after a break from defence and his quick low cross could only be parried by goalkeeper Carl Rushworth for Saka to tap in.

Advertisement

Coventry, back in the Premier League after 25 years, had to stay patient as Arsenal dominated possession, but they came close at the end of the first half with a looping Loum Tchaouna overhead kick that had keeper David Raya scrambling to get back. Arsenal effectively killed the game off four minutes into the second period when captain Odegaard grabbed a third with a scuffed finish that wrong-footed Rushworth. Loading Coventry could have nicked a consolation goal with five minutes to go when a cross found Jack Rudoni unmarked, but he could only head into Raya’s arms. “There was a lot to like in the performance and obviously it’s a great result,” Arteta said afterwards. “The manner in which we started with such domination, clarity, understanding and flow in the game it was really impressive.”

Advertisement

Arsenal last attempted to retain the Premier League title in 2004-05, eventually finishing a distant second behind Chelsea; no Gunners ​team have successfully defended the top-flight title since they won three in a row ending in 1935. Related Article Analysis

Premier League Can anyone stop Arsenal? That and five other big Premier League storylines to follow This time around, they are starting their campaign as one of the few clubs untouched by a close season of managerial upheaval at many of their rivals – including Manchester City and Liverpool. They have also spent heavily again on signings and Arteta is likely to have been particularly encouraged by the form of winger Tzolis. The Greek international was a non-stop threat on the left-hand side, working up and down all game and beating Coventry’s defenders on both the outside and when cutting in.

Advertisement

Tzolis hustled to initially win the ball for Havertz’s goal, crossed the ball for Saka to score the second, went close himself on a number of occasions and was given a standing ovation when he was replaced by Eberechi Eze after 76 minutes. Loading Arsenal captain Odegaard heaped praise on Tzolis. “Amazing, he played a brilliant game,” he said. “He has been brilliant all pre-season. He’s so lively, it’s hard to defend him. He’s a really intelligent player, he always looks up and finds the right pass.” Coventry manager Frank Lampard said it had been a tough introduction to the Premier League for his players.

“It’s a big learning curve for the players today,” he said. “Arsenal away will not define our season, it absolutely won’t. But taking on the lessons absolutely will.” Reuters News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

Roosters captain James Tedesco has been ruled out of the clash with Wests Tigers, extending his time on the sidelines to a month. Tedesco has taken longer than expected to recover from an ankle injury he suffered in round 22 and is a late scratching for Sunday’s clash at Allianz Stadium. Roosters star James Tedesco has again been ruled out. Getty Images “No, he won’t play,” Roosters coach Trent Robinson said. “It’s more than the ankle - it’s been a bit frustrating for Ted. We’ve named him each week, but he’s not right to play this week. He’s progressed quite well, but it’s a bit more niggling than what we thought.” Robinson said he would again name Tedesco for next week’s clash with the Dolphins and was hopeful he would be ready to return.

“The longer you go [on the sidelines], the more you have to train before you get back,” Robinson said. “In the first week, it could have easily been one session, but now he has to build up almost a whole week of training, and he hasn’t been able to do that. We’re getting close, but yeah, he won’t play.” The Roosters are on the lookout for two assistants after Matt King accepted the NSW State of Origin job, while Michael Cheika will return to the Waratahs in Super Rugby. While Cheika will soon turn his attention to the 15-man game, Robinson predicted it wouldn’t preclude him from achieving his ambition of becoming an NRL head coach. “I don’t think so,” Robinson said. “We took on the boldness at the Roosters to take somebody from the outside ... there are different angles that you need to have a look at in our game. Our game’s getting big enough. “Cheika coached Lebanon at the World Cup, he’s now done his second stint here at the Roosters, and he’s a head coach - that’s his ultimate background. I don’t think it precludes him from being a head [NRL] coach; I actually think what he’s done this year puts him at the front of the queue for when a job does come up. He’s decided to go back to the sport that he loves, but I think we’ve added one of those sports to his list as well.”

The former Manly captain will finish his career at Bath in the English Super League. “It’s been wonderful being able to coach Daly this year and seeing the value add he’s had in our group,” Robinson said. Bath-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans. Thomas Wielecki “He’s come on, and I love the fact that he and Sam [Walker] have been really tight and close. The unlikely mentors helping Marshall at Tigers Adrian Proszenko A cricket icon, a basketball coach and an AFL legend are among the mentors Benji Marshall is leaning on to help him through the toughest period of his storied career. Wests Tigers are on an eight-game losing streak as they come up against a Roosters side at Allianz Stadium on Sunday that has won eight consecutive games.

The club is languishing in 14th place and is still technically a chance of earning the wooden spoon if they remain winless for the remainder of the season and other results conspire against them. Veteran South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has long been a sounding board for Marshall, who revealed he is also seeking advice from Perth Wildcats NBL head coach John Rillie, former Australian cricketer Mike Hussey and Adelaide Crows coach Matthew Nicks. “One thing I don’t really talk about is that I have a lot of people I can lean on – coaches, ex-coaches, ex-players, and people in business,” Marshall said on Friday. “What [Bennett and I] talk about is pretty private between us, but he’s just so good to talk to. When you’ve got guys who have been through the same thing and understand what it is, that’s helpful. Benji Marshall. Kate Geraghty

“I’ve also got a leadership group I’m in called Leader. They run these courses, and I’ve got four head coaches from other sports in my group … We run a lot of things by each other, which is really helpful because they’re in similar situations in different sports and go through the same stuff.” Asked if there was any advice that resonated, Marshall said: “For me, it’s a constant journey of learning and evolving. Obviously, I got thrown in with little experience and had to ride through a few things in the first three years that a lot of people don’t go through in their whole career. “But you’ve got to grow from it, learn from it, and be more ready to deal with things in the future if they come about again. You just have to keep learning. It’s tough, I’ll be honest, but at the same time, there’s no other job in the world where I’d get as much purpose as I get from doing what I’m doing right now. “I get to help young men not only play footy, but become better people. Despite long being out of finals contention, the Red V has continued to be competitive as the end of the season draws nearer. “I spoke about that after the game,” Marshall said. “I thought [Dragons coach] Dean [Young] has done a really good job with them given the circumstances of how they started and what happened with their coach and what not. “One thing that’s been clear – even though they’re near the bottom of the table – is the way they’re playing doesn’t reflect that. Cogger also received a $3000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash. Kevin Walters celebrates Ashes victory with Cameron Munster and Angus Crichton in 2025. The coach will finish up as Kangaroos coach after the World Cup. Storm veteran announces medical retirement after suffering stroke Storm prop and Fijian Test captain Tui Kamikamica has announced his medically forced retirement from rugby league after suffering a stroke earlier this year. Kamikamica hasn’t played since April when he suffered a seizure in the middle of the night and underwent subsequent surgery to remove a blood clot. ‘Proud day for NRL’: Storm valued at $150m after sale goes through Adrian Proszenko The Melbourne Storm has been valued at more than $150 million after the world’s second-biggest investment firm bought a majority share of the club.
