Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Aussie 'paradox'

When Steven's sister Christina Law discovered that her grandmother would feature in Drew's poster collection, she was moved to tears.

"I was really overwhelmed and quite teary when I saw that nanna had been included in this series," Christina told SBS Chinese.

The posters feature archival photographs, sourced from the National Archives of Australia (NAA) of people who applied for certificates exempting them from the dictation test.

Under the Immigration Restriction Act 1901, one of the laws that formed part of what is now known as the White Australia policy, the dictation test could be administered at an officer's discretion to people seeking entry to Australia.

It required a person to write a 50-word passage in a European language dictated by an immigration officer. After 1905, the officer could choose "any prescribed language", making it possible to administer the test in a language the person did not understand.

People who failed were declared a "prohibited immigrant" and refused entry or , in some circumstances, deported.

The exemption certificates were designed to allow eligible non-European residents who had lived in Australia to leave temporarily and return within a set timeframe without being subjected to the dictation test.

People applying for the exemption from the dictation test were generally required to demonstrate they were of good character and produce written references. Source: SBS News / National Archives of Australia

It's been more than a decade since Drew debuted the poster series in 2016.

The posters have since sparked mixed reactions, including graffiti, counter-posters and attempts to tear them down.

In recent months, videos of the artworks being defaced and altered to include different messages about identity have also circulated on social media.

"Someone has vandalised my old posters, so I've got some new ones, and I'm going to fix them up," Drew told SBS Chinese while standing on Morphett Street in Adelaide's central business district.

He's equipped with a canvas rucksack full of supplies and replaces the graffitied artworks with the ease of someone who has installed thousands of posters over the years.

Peter Drew has spent more than a decade producing, installing and often replacing his iconic Aussie posters. Source: SBS News / George Chan

Asked whether the "Aussie" label on his posters is a question or statement, Drew said there's no simple answer.

"In some ways, the posters have a double meaning because the first way to read it is that the person in the poster is Aussie, and that's a celebration of them being Australian," he said.

"But in another way, the poster is also saying that the White Australia policy is Aussie, and that's something that we don't celebrate. So, there is a paradox because those two things are conflicting with each other."

For Steven and Christina, the posters illuminate a chapter of their family's history that remained largely shrouded in secrecy.

'We knew nothing'

In 1900, Irene (then known as Lucy Maud Lem Cue) was born in South Wangaratta in north-east Victoria.

Her biological mother was born in New Zealand and had British ancestry. Her father, Lem Cue, was of Chinese descent and died when Irene was two years old. She was then adopted by another Chinese-European family and raised in Melbourne.

At the age of 18, Irene travelled to Hong Kong with her adoptive father, who hoped to recruit workers for his furniture manufacturing business and expand his commercial interests in China.

In March 1921, she returned to Australia and obtained a Certificate Exemption from Dictation Test (CEDT) before travelling back to Hong Kong.

Irene would eventually marry and raise children — mostly on her own, after her husband's death.

In the 1970s, Irene returned permanently to Melbourne, where she remained until she died at age 80.

READ MORE A dark chapter of Australia's past is resurfacing in immigration politics

Despite her overseas travels, Irene was born in Australia and therefore considered a British subject by birth (Australian citizenship was later introduced in 1949). That legal status, however, did not necessarily protect people of Chinese and other non-European backgrounds from immigration restrictions.

But historian Michael Williams believes people of Chinese ancestry were "overwhelmingly" targeted by Australian immigration officials during this period.

"Legally, yes, they were definitely Australians. But socially, it was a bit more problematic," Williams told SBS Chinese.

"If they grew up looking Chinese, then they would not have been considered Australian. The White Australia policy pretty much identified an Australian as being a white person."

Michael Williams has long studied Chinese-Australian history, including the impacts of the White Australia policy. Source: SBS News / George Chan

When Steven discovered that his grandmother's records had been preserved by the NAA, he felt a "stronger" connection to his family's past but admits he also felt angry.

"Irene never spoke to us about the difficulties she had. We knew nothing about that until after she passed away.

"We were a bit angry in a way, that these people were Australians; they were Australian-born, yet they needed these documents in order to return to the country."

The White Australia policy and its legacy

According to the NAA, only a "small number" of people were granted CEDTs. Those exemptions could allow non-European residents to travel overseas and return to Australia, while those who were not exempted could face exclusion.

The dictation test was administered 1,359 times before 1909, with only 52 people granted entry, according to the NAA. After 1909, no migrants required to sit the test passed.

Williams said he has seen examples of dictation tests in which immigration officers targeted people from multicultural backgrounds who understood English.

"If you happened to speak English, they would test you in Greek or Estonian at one stage ... and as a result of failing the test ... you were [considered living] illegally in Australia and could be put in jail."

READ MORE Those in Australia feel the shift. Those outside are watching closely

The dictation test was abolished in 1958, but elements of the White Australia policy remained in place for years afterwards. The final remnants of the policy were removed in 1973, while the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 subsequently made racial discrimination unlawful in areas covered by the legislation.

Christina said she learnt about the mechanisms of the White Australia policy at school, but for a long time, did not realise how this history personally impacted her.

"I see now that it relates to me. I mean that was why we were the only Asian family in the school because no other Asians were allowed into the country at the time."

It was not until the 1980s, after Irene Law's death, that Steven and Christina started researching their family history. Source: SBS News / George Chan

Steven also remembers questioning his Australian identity at a young age.

"People called us names, we were teased, and we often felt isolated," he said.

Now 66, Steven said he feels "richer" because of his Chinese ancestry and cultural traditions passed down through generations.

His experience reflects a broader shift in the makeup of Australian society. About 731,500 people born in China lived in Australia in June 2025, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

The 2021 Census recorded more than 1.39 million people with Chinese ancestry, making it one of the largest overseas-born ancestry communities in the country.

When people from multicultural backgrounds walk the streets and spot Drew's brightly coloured posters, he hopes they are reminded that Australian identity "has room for them".

"It's not such a rigid thing that is set in the past and static, not evolving. It's actually ... much stronger ... than that."

Steven also believes the artworks continue to send a powerful reminder that people, no matter their background, are "welcome here, no matter where they're from".

"[Irene] was Aussie, just as much as we are. Just as much as the other people in the posters."

title: 'Left feeling like a burden': How the government's new NDIS changes may impact you
text:
In brief The government says its NDIS changes will save billions of dollars.

Advocates aren't convinced, saying the changes have left disabled Australians feeling like a burden.

An overhaul of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) has passed the Senate with Coalition support, sent back to the Labor-controlled lower house to be rubber-stamped.

Analysis by the Grattan Institute suggests hundreds of thousands of people will be moved off the scheme or prevented from joining under the changes.

Applicants will be assessed in stages under a new test to determine their functional capacity.

That test is still being developed and will replace the current diagnosis-based model.

Acting CEO of peak body People With Disability Australia Megan Spindler-Smith says her community is grieving.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"There will be harm, there will be injuries. What we're talking about here is that when you reduce people's access to the supports that they need to be able to get out of bed, access the community, go to work, you ostensibly isolate people."

She says many lives will be made smaller by the reforms — which will slash social and community participation supports in half.

"The support needs don't go away when the funding is cut or when the supports are removed. They just get pushed onto either systems or other people, and that means isolation."

Since it started in 2013, the cost of the scheme has ballooned, rising to $50 billion dollars this year, and projected to hit $100 billion within a decade.

The government says its overhaul will slow the scheme’s growth and save almost $38 billion over the next four years.

Greens MPs like Jordon Steele-John say the focus on financial cost has made many disabled people feel like a burden.

“Many people, during the course of this debate, while the government has been trying to push this legislation through, have shared with me that they have felt as though they are being talked about in a way that leaves them feeling like a burden, and that is just not okay.”

Health Minister Mark Butler says reining in spending growth was necessary to safeguard the scheme's financial sustainability and social license.

"This plan puts the scheme back on track, and I'm confident, secures it for decades to come," Butler said.

"It genuinely has transformed the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, and I want to continue to see that happen for decades to come. But we know also that we need to build supports for people who were never intended to be covered by the NDIS, people with more low to moderate support needs, those sorts of second-tier supports that were envisaged by the designers of this amazing reform."

After a snap Senate inquiry that received more than 4,500 submissions, amid sustained campaigning from advocates, the government cut a deal with the Coalition to pass the bill.

A total of 63 amendments were tabled across both houses, but Disability Program Director at the Grattan Institute Sam Bennett says those that passed are only minor in scope.

"I wouldn't say any of them are particularly significant, in all honesty. I think mostly they're pretty minor tweaks to the existing provisions within the Act. Many of them probably done by government to try and clarify their existing drafting.”

READ MORE Controversial NDIS changes get last-minute green light as Labor cuts deal with Coalition

The Coalition secured amendments to create new fraud offences, including penalties for NDIS providers that offer inducements or kickbacks.

The legislation also includes clearer guidance on what supports parents are expected to provide, clarifies rights to request re-assessment, and boosts whistleblower protections.

After pressure from the Greens, the government added to explanatory material clarifying a requirement for applicants to seek all appropriate treatment before being eligible for the NDIS.

Spindler-Smith says it was a significant win.

"What we now have is some really strong clarification that things like restrictive practices, and that's anything that limits the rights and freedom of movement for people with disability — and that could include seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint, or environmental restraint — those things are being clarified that they are not part of that because in theory, they could fit under all appropriate treatment."

"And the requirements for someone to access the NDIS would have been really problematic if they had been one of the requirements under the all appropriate treatment."

Another amendment clarifies the scope of ministerial powers that will allow social and community supports to be cut, while safeguarding other supports for participants with the highest needs.

READ MORE Government admits NDIS reforms will impact families, downplays fears over state readiness

"We see that as something that will make sure that people who do require 24-hour support and care are not going to be impacted in the same way, because there were some real concerns," Spindler-Smith said.

The focus will now shift to programs being created by the states and territories, which will be responsible for providing alternative supports from January 2028.

They'll be funded through a five-year, $10 billion commitment, split evenly between state and territory governments and the Commonwealth.

Most advanced at this stage is Thriving Kids, a $4 billion program for children with mild to moderate autism and developmental delays.

It’s meant to start in six weeks, and preparedness varies by jurisdiction, but despite agreeing in principle, Queensland is yet to sign up.

Butler says he remains confident alternative supports will be put in place.

"That's the deal that we've struck with states and territories," Butler said. "Thriving Kids is well underway. Implementation plans have been agreed with all states and territories except Queensland, which frankly needs to get its act together. But all other states and territories have implementation plans in place to build them. They'll be in place before the before the first of January, I'm very confident."

But he acknowledges much of the design and delivery of this overhaul is yet to come.

"We have a ton of work to do on other population groups, so kids over the age of nine, adults with more low to moderate support needs. We've got a lot of work to do with states and territories, but we've got time to do that. We've got the commitment of all states, premiers and chief ministers signed that deal with the prime minister earlier this year. We've got money allocated. We now just have to get on with the job."

A technical working group will provide advice to government on the new assessment tool this year and into next.

The new legislation is due to undergo statutory review within five years.

Obviously, I got thrown in with little experience and had to ride through a few things in the first three years that a lot of people don’t go through in their whole career. “But you’ve got to grow from it, learn from it, and be more ready to deal with things in the future if they come about again. You just have to keep learning. It’s tough, I’ll be honest, but at the same time, there’s no other job in the world where I’d get as much purpose as I get from doing what I’m doing right now. “I get to help young men not only play footy, but become better people. If I reflect on the first half of the season, there were signs there that we’ve got enough to do it. We just need to make sure that it doesn’t get away from us again like it did this year.” ‘Obviously, I got thrown in with little experience and had to ride through a few things in the first three years that a lot of people don’t go through in their whole career.’ Benji Marshall

Advertisement

Marshall said his side would do well to learn from St George Illawarra, who narrowly defeated them last weekend. Despite long being out of finals contention, the Red V has continued to be competitive as the end of the season draws nearer. “I spoke about that after the game,” Marshall said. “I thought [Dragons coach] Dean [Young] has done a really good job with them given the circumstances of how they started and what happened with their coach and what not. “One thing that’s been clear – even though they’re near the bottom of the table – is the way they’re playing doesn’t reflect that. They’ve knocked off some pretty handy opponents and taken all of their last six games to the wire. That comes through hard work, determination, fight, and pride in the jersey, and it’s similar for us.” Cogger ban set to stretch into finals AAP

Advertisement

Penrith are in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart on Thursday night. Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals. Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole. Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers’ 22-14 win on Thursday night. Penrith’s Jack Cogger is facing a three-week suspension for this tackle on Thursday night. Nine

Advertisement

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney’s Ashton Ward. If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season. Cogger also received a $3000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash. But the 29-year-old’s suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish. Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers’ starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

Advertisement

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith’s comeback victory in the 2023 grand final. But Cogger’s illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week’s clash with Canterbury. Walters’ surprise Kangaroos exit opens up next option for Ivan Cleary Dan Walsh Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters will exit the role after this year’s World Cup, bringing four-time premiership-winning Panthers mentor Ivan Cleary into contention to take charge of the national side.

Advertisement

Walters will lead Australia’s World Cup defence in October before moving to England, where he will be head coach of St Helens on what sources have indicated is a deal worth more than $600,000 a year. Kevin Walters celebrates Ashes victory with Cameron Munster and Angus Crichton in 2025. The coach will finish up as Kangaroos coach after the World Cup. NRL Photos Cleary looms large among contenders to replace Walters in charge of the Kangaroos given he will vacate the Panthers head coaching role at the end of 2027, handing the reigns to assistant Peter Wallace. The likes of recent Queensland Origin coach Billy Slater, NSW counterpart Laurie Daley and Australia’s most-capped player, Cameron Smith are other options for the national side. But Cleary will prove hard to look past given his CV and stated desire to get into representative coaching once finishing up in the NRL.

Advertisement

Cleary spoke openly of his interest in coaching either Australia or NSW in an interview with this masthead last year. While Matt King’s two-year deal to lead the Blues (with an automatic third year triggered by a series win) takes the NSW Origin role off the table, Walters’ early exit from the Kangaroos opens up an unexpected avenue for Cleary. Panthers coach Ivan Cleary. Louise Kennerley “I have thought about it a bit more lately, I don’t know why,” Cleary said last November. “I’m not sure whether I really want to or not, but it’s starting to intrigue me a little bit more, yeah. “Today I’ve just come back after being around the Australian camp. There’s something pretty cool about coaching the best players, good players with guys from other teams that I’ve coached against. It’s a different dynamic.

Advertisement

“Just the whole thing where you don’t have a lot of time [to prepare] and so that’s something I haven’t really done much of. I was assistant coach of the Kiwis in a World Cup, I really enjoyed that as well. One of the things I really liked about it was working with guys from other teams and just trying to get a team together quickly.” There is no immediate rush for the ARL Commission to replace Walters given the Kangaroos will not play again after the World Cup until the end of 2027. Cleary would have coached his last game with Penrith by that point, though he will remain on the club’s books in a consultancy role. Billy Slater is a free agent once more. Getty Images. Australia will open their World Cup campaign against New Zealand on October 15, aiming for a fourth consecutive tournament victory dating back to 2008. Walters will exit the Kangaroos’ role 12 months early, having signed a two-year extension in June. He led Australia to a 3-0 Ashes victory over England last year after Smith and former NSW Origin mentor Brad Fittler were considered for the national role.

Advertisement

Fittler withdrew from the race believing he could not do the Australian job justice due to his media commitments. Despite being repeatedly touted as a replacement for Craig Bellamy at Melbourne, Slater has consistently said he is not interested in becoming an NRL head coach. Related Article NRL 2026 Cronulla star avoids conviction for mooning park ranger, vows to ‘keep my pants up’ He walked away from the Maroons job on Friday after five years in charge, declaring: “It’s the right time for someone else to come in and lead our footy team.” Speaking on The Sunday Footy, Slater hinted that he would consider a potential return as Queensland coach in the future, though the pressure and time commitments of Origin campaigns also played a role in his departure.

Advertisement

Smith has ruled himself out of contention to replace Slater and lead the Maroons, saying the Origin workload would also be too much for him. The pressure in the Australian job is not as great and the workload is less, given the international calendar is now confined to after the NRL season. With Queensland Origin assistant Ben Te’o weighing up a move to South Sydney next season, Broncos assistant Matt Ballin has emerged as a leading contender to take charge of the Maroons. Souths make call on Latrell Mitchell’s comeback plan Christian Nicolussi

Advertisement

Latrell Mitchell’s long-awaited return for the Rabbitohs has been delayed for another week, but South Sydney’s highest-paid player is closing in on a comeback and much-needed game time leading into the finals. Coach Wayne Bennett had raised hopes of Mitchell playing his first game since round 10 when he was included in the Rabbitohs extended squad for Saturday’s clash against the Warriors, with Bennett telling this masthead Mitchell was “a chance” if he could complete full training this week. Latrell Mitchell at South Sydney training earlier this week. Steven Siewert But Souths have opted to keep their superstar centre on ice for another week. They also confirmed there have been no setbacks in his recovery from an ongoing nerve issue in his lower back. The nerve damage was linked to subsequent upper leg and calf problems for Mitchell which ruled him out of NSW’s Origin campaign. The Rabbitohs have targeted next week’s round 26 match against the Titans for Mitchell to return to the paddock, though that is still contingent on him handling increased training loads.

Advertisement

Bennett has flagged a potential bench role for Mitchell, who is unlikely to be played for a full 80 minutes against either the Gold Coast or arch-rivals the Roosters in the final round of the regular season. The Warriors, meanwhile, have announced the re-signing of coach Andrew Webster on a new four-year deal that will keep him at the club until the end of 2032. The extension will see Webster’s tenure at the high-flying Kiwi side stretch out to a decade, and make him the longest-serving coach in club history. Storm veteran announces medical retirement after suffering stroke Storm prop and Fijian Test captain Tui Kamikamica has announced his medically forced retirement from rugby league after suffering a stroke earlier this year. Kamikamica hasn’t played since April when he suffered a seizure in the middle of the night and underwent subsequent surgery to remove a blood clot. Further tests revealed he had a small hole in his heart, which was then closed in another operation.

Advertisement

Kamikamica, 32, is in good health and had hoped to return to playing, either in the NRL or via a move to the Super League. He will instead now call time on his 142-game career with Melbourne, which included grand final appearances in 2024 and 2025 and was acknowledged with being inducted as a life member of the club on Monday night. Tui Kamikamica has medically retired. NRL Photos “I’m incredibly proud of everything I’ve been able to achieve in the game, representing Storm and captaining my country,” Kamikamica said. “To play for the Storm and captain Fiji are memories I’ll cherish forever. I want to thank everyone at the Storm for believing in me and giving me the opportunity to play at the highest level. Melbourne will always be a special place for me and my family and I’m looking forward to my next chapter in life.”

Advertisement

‘I wish I got injured instead of him’: Brotherly love ahead of Trbojevic comeback Adrian Proszenko Jake Trbojevic has paid tribute to brother Tom as he embarks on another comeback, saying most players in his position would have written off the year. Tom Trbojevic is a huge addition to a Manly side that remains a mathematical possibility of squeaking into the finals if they beat Newcastle at McDonald Jones Stadium on Saturday.

Advertisement

The Sea Eagles haven’t won a game since their captain suffered his latest hamstring injury, in round 20. However, the fullback will be a welcome addition to a side that has lost halfback Joey Walsh to a fractured jaw. Another Trbojevic, youngest sibling Ben, also returns from injury. “I’ll be honest, it is tough, it’s really tough,” Jake Trbojevic said about playing without Tom. “I’ve got a lot of respect for Tom, obviously being my brother and all that, but the way he goes about things – he is a true professional. “Everyone says that about people, but he genuinely is. Sometimes I wish it was me who got injured instead of him, because he puts in 10 times more work than anyone else to get his body right, and he’s just been very unlucky. Tom Trbojevic, Jake Trbojevic and Ben Trbojevic Getty Images

Advertisement

“It’s very hard to see, particularly being his older brother. Not only that, selfishly I want him out on the field because he makes us better, you know? So, it is tough, but I’m happy for him that he’s very resilient and keeps working hard. These things don’t hold him back. “A lesser man would probably say, ‘You know what, I’ll just sit the year out and come back next year,’ but he’s fighting. He wants to be out there, he wants to lead this club, and that’s great.” If Tom Trbojevic’s return is successful he could put himself into contention for Australia selection for the end-of-year World Cup. Much will depend on how he and Manly perform in coming weeks, although it’s unlikely the club will feature in the post-season. “There’s always a chance,” Jake Trbojevic said. “Tom wants to play for Manly, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line, he wants to be out there. He’s the captain of this club for a reason, and we love having him out there. The Northern Beaches loves having him out there. We’re better for it. Tom Trbojevic. Getty

Advertisement

“So, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line—whether it’s finals or no finals—we want him out there, he wants to be out there, and he works extremely hard, so he deserves to be out there. We’re going to go out there, put in a great performance, and he’s going to lead us well. Hopefully, we can keep improving and turn this around.” Manly winger Jason Saab said Tom Trbojevic’s return would give the team a confidence boost. “He’s a world-class player,” Saab said. “He’s had a tough run with injuries this year, but whenever he’s been fit and played the full game, he’s always had an impact. “We’re a better team when the Trbojevics are playing.”

Advertisement

‘Proud day for NRL’: Storm valued at $150m after sale goes through Adrian Proszenko The Melbourne Storm has been valued at more than $150 million after the world’s second-biggest investment firm bought a majority share of the club. After an exhaustive process to find the right partner, the Storm has completed a landmark transaction with EQT, a Swedish firm with more than $333 billion in assets under management. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images

Advertisement

The sale puts the Storm alongside Collingwood and the Brisbane Broncos as one of Australia’s top sporting franchises, just after the NRL brokered a $5.3 billion broadcast deal. Storm chair Matt Tripp – who remains a co-owner alongside Bart Campbell, Gerry Ryan, Tom Carroll and Brett Ralph – said the deal will elevate one of Australia’s top-performing sports clubs even higher. “I’m really proud that a firm like EQT, who are a serious blue-chip investment company, has chosen us as the team in Australia that they want to invest in,” Tripp said. “That’s a credit to our people and the work that’s gone on over the last 27 years and the 13 years I’ve been involved as a club. “I’ve watched people work tirelessly at the Storm. Off the back of that, EQT recognised that and wanted to be part of that. It’s a really proud day for the club and the NRL more broadly. I think the NRL should be happy that a club has attracted the attention of a company like EQT.”

Advertisement

The deal, which will result in EQT earning board seats, is subject to Australian Rugby League Commission approval. Tripp will remain chair, while other key positions will remain the same. Related Article NRL 2026 Why a top-two finish by the NZ Warriors could cost NRL $3m “Absolutely status quo,” Tripp said. “I’m still the largest shareholder after EQT and I’m as committed as I’ve ever been. It wouldn’t matter if I owned one per cent of 100 per cent, I’m still as passionate and my desire to drive this club doesn’t waiver … “These guys own the IMG Academy, which will be really beneficial for us. “It’s one of the biggest academies in the world, they effectively groom and produce through their pathways academy in the US the best of the best in gridiron, basketball, baseball and the like.

Advertisement

“In terms of sports science and everything that goes on that is best in class, we feel we can benefit from that and our new partners will assist us. “They are also huge investors in the AI space and data and hopefully some of that can be transformed into improving areas of the club.” No Red V lifeline as Sloan seeks Super League answers Dan Walsh Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan says he has been “left in the dark” about the future of Castleford coach Ryan Carr, as St George Illawarra rule out extending an NRL lifeline to him and teammates Damien Cook and Mat Feagai if they look to back out of their Super League deals.

Advertisement

Sloan conceded after the Dragons’ two-point win over Wests Tigers on Sunday that he has had second thoughts about his move to Castleford given the uncertainty around Carr’s position. Carr was a key reason Sloan signed a two-year deal with the club last month. Carr, who coached Sloan as an assistant and interim head coach at the Dragons, has been absent from Castleford for the past two weeks after the club launched an investigation into the 38-year-old with little detail or public explanation as to why. Castleford head of football Chris Chester has spoken to the Dragons trio and told them they remain in the club’s plans for next season regardless of Carr’s situation. Loading St George Illawarra have moved on in their roster planning for 2027 and have privately conveyed that they do not have room for Sloan, Cook and Feagai in their salary cap after a significant recruitment and retention spree.

Advertisement

“It definitely puts a big dent in things for me, I’ll be honest,” Sloan said. “Carry was a big reason why I signed over there. “Obviously we had a relationship here at the Dragons and I don’t really know the situation with him. We’ve been left in the dark. “I’m really excited to go over there if Carry is there, but I just don’t know if that’s going to be the case there. Hopefully I’ll find out soon what’s going on and they make a decision. Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan. Getty Images “I have thought about [trying to stay in the NRL], but I also have to keep playing good footy here to finish the season on a high.”

Sloan, 24, has been playing with a new lease on life since Dean Young took charge of the Dragons, scoring eight tries in his past eight games. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Twelve months ago, the Knights were heading for the wooden spoon. Holbrook must be coach of the year Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist His time under predecessor Shane Flanagan was far less consistent with several demotions to reserve grade, and 18 months ago he was given permission to explore an early exit from the joint-venture. Immortal Andrew Johns has argued Sloan is “too good a player to be leaving the NRL at this age”, but the Indigenous All Stars representative acknowledged his form in previous years hadn’t left him with many options. “I didn’t really have much [many options] in the NRL, and nothing really made sense, you know, to play in another jersey in the NRL,” Sloan said.

“But Joey’s always been really good to me since I came into first grade and to be getting a fair rap from someone who has done everything in the game, I hold that in such respect. At the moment, I’ve got the Super League deal and at the end of it, I’ll only be 26. I’ve been in first grade since I was 18 so no matter what happens, I’d say I’ve got a lot of NRL left in me.”

title: It’s raining stars on big red mountain
text:
Advertisement

WorldAsiaChina It’s raining stars on big red mountain Lisa Visentin August 22, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Dahongshan, China: A sparkling night sky deep in the red dirt desert of Inner Mongolia is one of the more spectacular, if unexpected, backdrops to an invocation of Immanuel Kant. On a stretch of untamed escarpment dotted with camping tents and hand-dug toilets near China’s northern border, the German philosopher’s musings on the “starry heavens above and the moral law within” have been dropped into casual conversation. A group of families and friends from China’s Hebei province watch the Perseid meteor shower at Dahongshan in China’s Inner Mongolia region. Fairfax Media “There are only two things in the world that truly move people – one is the lofty moral standard in our hearts, and the other is the brilliant starry sky above our heads,” a camper tells me, paraphrasing Kant’s famous line from his 1788 Critique of Practical Reason.

Advertisement

“Ever since I was a child, I’ve heard that saying,” she adds. “It has always deeply moved me.” Our quoter works in the education bureau of central China’s Hebei province and has used the cover of the school holidays to slip away for a long weekend, unbeknownst to her bosses, so she declines to give her name. The red clay clifftops of Dahongshan in Inner Mongolia are popular with China’s stargazers. Fairfax Media The chance to see the Perseid meteor shower rain down over the Inner Mongolian sky was too good to miss, so she persuaded six friends and their four children to accompany her. They took three cars, packed them with camping gear, and drove 900 kilometres north. “When we were kids growing up in the countryside, we used to see the stars clearly. Children today basically have almost no chance to experience that,” the stargazer says.

Advertisement

“That’s why I believe that besides Chinese language, maths and other academic subjects, they also need some education about nature in their lives.” For the same reason, accountant Li Dan and her husband loaded their two children into their electric four-wheel-drive and set out for the desert from Wuhan in Hubei province, a multi-day drive. A meteor streaks across the sky above a Mongolian herder’s house in Dahongshan. Fairfax Media “Living in the city, we rarely get to see stars. This year, it’s a rare opportunity because it’s a new moon,” Li says, adding that previous years were spoiled by bad weather. I, too, have come to see the Perseid show and to chat with the stargazers who have trekked across the country to watch. It is an annual cosmic event best seen in the northern hemisphere around August, when Earth passes through the dust trail left by the comet Swift-Tuttle.

Advertisement

What look like shooting stars streaking across the night sky are actually rock particles burning up as they smash into Earth’s atmosphere. “I find work so exhausting in recent years. Getting out once in a while to stroll around and gaze at this vast, open starry sky just makes me feel so much more at ease,” says Wang Chunxu, a 25-year-old teacher from Beijing. “I feel like all my worries are melting away.” Li Dan (right) cooks dinner for her daughter and son as they wait for nightfall in Inner Mongolia. Fairfax Media This year, the confluence of a new moon (minimal light) and a near-perfect weather forecast conspired to make Dahongshan – literally, “big red mountain” – in Inner Mongolia, a region in northern China bordering the country of Mongolia, one of the best places in the world to watch the Perseid shower. To get there from Beijing, it’s an eight-hour drive north, a journey I made with a Chinese friend and his family.

Advertisement

We cut through the mountain ranges that frame the capital, before gradually climbing 1000 metres above sea level along a road that winds through the yurt-studded grasslands, home to ethnic Mongolian herders. From there, it’s onwards to the fringe of the Gobi Desert. After pausing for a herd of camels to cross the road, we reached the clifftop of Dahongshan in time to see the sun set over a sweeping escarpment of chiselled rocky hills and red clay plateau as far as the eye can see. A herd of two-humped camels roam across the grasslands of China’s Inner Mongolia region. Fairfax Media Chalk it up to a touch of homesickness, but I’m reminded of the hot ochre of central Australia – more Dorothea Mackellar than Kant in my mind. By the time we arrived, dozens of campers had already claimed their spots on the clifftop and were setting up tripods and cameras, or cooking over electric stoves rigged up to their EVs.

Advertisement

Among them was a gaggle of 12 strangers aged in their 20s to 40s from Beijing and Tianjin, who were wrangled by Zhang Yang, a calligraphy tutor when he is not hitting the open roads. Zhang put a call-out on Douyin (the Chinese TikTok) to anyone who wanted to join him on a road trip to watch the meteor shower, so long as they split the cost of petrol, tolls and food. A group of young people take aerial photos with a drone at Dahongshan. Fairfax Media He says he got the bug for the great outdoors after watching Australian outback documentaries as a boy. “Australians drove utes and travelled around. I found those documentaries quite fascinating. Now, I travel all over the country but prefer places with fewer tourists,” Zhang says.

Advertisement

“This is my first time observing a meteor shower under such good weather conditions.” Related Article North Korea Kimchi and a show: Inside a North Korean restaurant in Beijing We wait until about 9pm for the sky to become dark enough for the first stars to appear, and then suddenly it’s radiant. A shimmering Milky Way from horizon to horizon. Necks craned skywards, gasps and squeals erupt across the campsite as the first meteors blitz across the sky. The dedicated will stay up past 2am to catch as many as 90 luminous streaks. The ideal setting to contemplate the humbling vastness of the universe, and humanity’s moral imperative to try to make sense of it. title: ‘He’s a world-class operator’: How the Cheika deal to return to the Waratahs was done
text:

Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘He’s a world-class operator’: How the Cheika deal to return to the Waratahs was done Iain Payten August 22, 2026 — 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sepia-toned sugar hit, or seismic change under a world-class coach? That’s the debate emerging over Michael Cheika’s return to the Waratahs as head coach for, at least, the 2027 season. Following a three-week flurry of negotiations between Cheika and Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh, the 59-year-old agreed to return to NSW a dozen years after leading the franchise to its one and only Super Rugby title in 2014. Michael Cheika will take the reins at the Waratahs for the second time in his career. AP It will be a reunion, of sorts, with two key members of that Waratahs side – Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps – having also recently re-signed with the outfit for 2027, and with Stephen Hoiles the frontrunner to become a senior assistant coach under Cheika, and his likely successor in 2028. Another 2014 alumni, Wycliff Palu, is also in the mix to return as an assistant coach.

Advertisement

The jokes have been flowing online about getting the 2014 Tahs band back together, but those relationships were instrumental in Cheika returning, according to informed sources familiar with how the deal was done. After Dan McKellar exited in June, the Tahs and RA – which owns the franchise – called for applications. Cheika did not apply but after senior NSW players reached out to raise the possibility of him also returning with Foley and Phipps, a meeting with RA was set up. Michael Cheika and Michael Hooper celebrate victory over the Crusaders in the Super Rugby decider in 2014. Getty Images Talks between Cheika and Waugh progressed, and terms were agreed. Cheika remains connected emotionally to the Waratahs, and the timing worked. The former Wallabies coach has been pursuing a head coach gig in the NRL but missed out on the Eels job last year, and the Dragons vacancy earlier this year. A return to head coaching in rugby – where he remains in demand among major Test nations and the world’s biggest clubs – was always on.

Advertisement

With the likelihood of high-profile head coaching jobs in international rugby opening up after the 2027 Rugby World Cup, the former Randwick coach agreed to return to the Tahs for at least the next season, and with the option to stay in 2028. Informed sources believe it is likely Cheika will only coach NSW for one season before handing over to his successor, but there is some hope once he is in the door and invested, the temptation to see out the mission may be too great. The probable brevity of Cheika’s return has drawn critics, however, who argue it is another “sugar hit” for a club with a bad habit of chopping and changing coaches. Others say returning coaches rarely recapture the success of their first stint. Michael Cheika, pictured here in 2022, is back at the Tahs. Oscar Colman But Rugby Australia chairman Daniel Herbert is adamant the return of Cheika will be a huge boost for the Waratahs – and rugby in general – regardless of his length of stay, and said the fact he may only be on deck one year was never a problem.

Advertisement

“We went in knowing that was going to be the case. We went in at the very start – it was mentioned in the very first conversation – that we were aware of that,” Herbert said. “In an ideal world, you could guarantee that second year, but you also know that a person of that calibre wants to coach internationally. “With what he’s been able to achieve in different programs, he can achieve a hell of a lot and help everyone at NSW Rugby knock things into shape. His impact will be felt well beyond now. “There is a second year, and we hope that he would want to stay for that second year, but really, we went in knowing that’s an option. If it works out, great; if it doesn’t (stay), we’ll be in far better shape than what we were without him. We are thrilled.”

Advertisement

Heading into a Rugby World Cup year, and with the tournament being played in Australia, the sense of urgency at RA for the Waratahs to rediscover success – and re-engage the country’s biggest market – was highlighted by the exit of McKellar, with a year remaining on his contract. Some of the biggest salaries in Australian rugby are held by Tahs players, including Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Angus Bell and the incoming Angus Crichton, but crowds have been steadily falling in recent years, with the Tahs having not made the finals since 2023. Cheika’s reputation as a turnaround specialist – proven many times – was therefore attractive. “He’s a world-class operator, and he’s shown that across multiple programs. If you look at who’s had the biggest impact on rugby, the greatest exports we’ve had in rugby from a coaching sense are him and Eddie. They’ve both achieved a hell of a lot,” Herbert said. Rugby Australia CEO Phil Waugh, who led the Cheika negotiatioons, and RA chair Daniel Herbert. Getty Images

Advertisement

“There are a lot of other young coaches coming through in lots of different programs, but to have Michael here and motivated about coaching the Waratahs again, getting them in good shape there, that’s great news. He’ll start to mentor some younger coaches as well. “It’s a great boon for Australian rugby, but in particular for every Waratahs and NSW rugby fan. It’s such an important market, and to have a person of that calibre, it’s just a great reunion.” Setting up a succession plan with Hoiles, or whoever wins the senior assistant job, eased concerns inside RA about the Cheika return being a short-term fix, and allowed it to be framed as a coaching solution that can pave the way for stability. Cheika is an assistant at the Roosters, and is often spotted in the cafe under the RA headquarters that the NRL club also frequent. Cheika addressed Roosters players on Wednesday ahead of the news being announced by the Waratahs. One small but significant part of the Cheika return, which could easily get lost, is the resumption of cordial relations between the coach and Rugby Australia.

Advertisement

Cheika’s exit from the Wallabies after the 2019 Rugby World Cup was messy, and saw a breakdown of relationships with then chief executive Raelene Castle and chair Cameron Clyne. Waugh was on the RA board at the time, but he was only new. Related Article New Zealand rugby Why New Zealand’s tour of South Africa could reshape modern rugby Cheika and Waugh met in February last year, when RA were searching for a successor to Joe Schmidt as Wallabies coach, but at the time head office wanted a continuity candidates, not a change agent, so Les Kiss got the nod. But a change is what is wanted at the Waratahs, and RA securing Cheika to be the agent has already proved valuable, with a mostly enthusiastic response from fans, media and players. “He is almost too big now for that job, to be honest,” one insider said, on the condition of anonymity. “They’ve done well to get him.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. “As I said very clearly on my return, I am not and never will be a Messiah; it will take a team effort.” So said John O’Neill in The Sun-Herald in 2009, two years into his second spell as chief executive of the Australian Rugby Union, as it was called then. The tenure proved more difficult than the first, and successful second comings in Australian rugby are a tricky business – Eddie Jones being the most recent piece of evidence. Michael Cheika will take the reins at the Waratahs for the second time in his career. AP So, while Michael Cheika’s return to the Waratahs is something to be welcomed – he’s one of the big beasts of the coaching jungle – it does come with a warning. It’s not as if O’Neill, Jones or Cheika lose the qualities that made them successful in the first instance. It’s that the world around them changes, and they return to jobs that are more complex and challenging than before.

Advertisement

Superficially, there are some similarities between Cheika’s first crack at the Waratahs and his second. Take a look at the Super Rugby ladder in 2012: the Waratahs finished third in the five-team Australian conference, but 23 competition points behind both the Reds and Brumbies with four wins and 12 losses. Michael Cheika at Waratahs training in 2013. Getty The Reds and Brumbies will again be Cheika’s big targets next year. In Cheika’s first year in charge in 2013, NSW again finished third in their conference, but they narrowed the gap considerably to the Reds and Brumbies, with eight wins and eight losses.

Advertisement

So, successfully chasing the Reds and Brumbies is familiar territory for Cheika. That challenge will spin his wheels because he is a very proud New South Welshman. But the landscape has changed since 2013 that Cheika is facing a bigger challenge, for two reasons. First, the Brumbies and Reds have established such successful programs in the intervening years that both clubs supply the No.9-No.10 combinations in the Wallabies squad. Second – and this is arguably the more significant point – the Western Force have emerged as a competitive force in Super Rugby Pacific with some of the better players in Australian rugby. If not for halfback Henry Robertson’s ACL injury, they too would have supplied a No.9-No.10 combination to the Wallabies squad.

Advertisement

Neither does the situation across the ditch offer much relief for Cheika. The Hurricanes have emerged as a powerhouse, the Chiefs have about a dozen All Blacks and the Crusaders have re-signed Richie Mo’unga. The Blues are in talks with Ardie Savea, too, and have landed the latest All Blacks No.8 Semisi Ta’eiloa. Kurtley Beale was part of a star-studded Waratahs team under Cheika in 2014. Photographic Cheika will understand this, of course, but he is returning to a competition in which the top six teams have virtually been set in stone for five years and there has been very little evidence of upward mobility: the “nearly” clubs in Super Rugby Pacific tend to remain that way. For that reason, Cheika’s second year is arguably going to be more important.

Advertisement

During his first spell, he made key signings such as Kurtley Beale and cult hero Jacques Potgieter for 2014 – acquisitions who made a massive difference to the title-winning year. But the contract announced by the Waratahs places a question mark on Cheika’s involvement beyond 2027. There is an “option” for 2028, but the fact it isn’t a straight two-year deal suggests both parties want to see how the sequel works out before committing to something longer. Setting impartiality aside, you would have to be pathologically negative towards the Waratahs not to wish Cheika success. The surge in Sydney crowd numbers towards the end of the 2014 Super Rugby campaign remains one of the competition’s highlights.

title: Steven King promised his team would be selfless, ruthless, connected. But there’s one word that defines his Demons

SportAFLAFL 2026 Steven King promised his team would be selfless, ruthless, connected. But there’s one word that defines his Demons Peter Ryan August 22, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Melbourne coach Steven King presented at a media briefing about the ambitions for his group in 2026, the coach’s optimism for the group’s immediate prospects was higher than most of the journalists in the room. King emphasised a pre-season based on high-speed running and vowed that the team would play a quick, modern style of football. Melbourne coach Steven King has built a strong rapport with his players in his first year at the helm. Getty He wanted the team to be selfless, ruthless and connected as they started their first year without either Christian Petracca, Clayton Oliver, and as it turned out, Steven May, on the list for the first time since 2015. The injured Jack Viney was unlikely to play much of a part in the season either.

Advertisement

The Demon dynasty anticipated in the afterglow of the 2021 premiership looked more like a failed state. A rebuild on the run seemed the most likely path as no one doubted the young talent at King’s disposal. View post on X The Demons’ recruiting team had not rested on the strategy Tim Lamb and Jason Taylor have employed to great effect for the past decade, with two first-round picks added to the list at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 national draft (they will have two first round picks again in 2026). But those players – Caleb Windsor and Koltyn Tholstrup (picks seven and 13, 2023), Harvey Langford and Xavier Lindsay (picks six and 11 in 2024), and Xavier Taylor and Latrelle Pickett (picks 11 and 12 in 2025) – had just 95 games experience between them when the siren sounded to kickstart round one.

Advertisement

And Max Gawn, Jake Lever and Ed Langdon shaped as the most likely contributors among the dozen players on the list aged above 30, with Brody Mihocek and Jack Steele recruited to keep them company over cups of tea. While King had impressed Melbourne’s coach selection panel, he remained a first-time coach, and no one was certain about how he would handle the hot seat. Now we know. King talks tough with his players. via Getty Images His coaching had an effect akin to running hot water over a tight jar lid, opening up a side of the Demons we had not seen. Under King, the blue-collar battlers have become the daring Demons, with their exhilarating upset win over ladder leaders Fremantle in round 22 making them genuine premiership contenders.

Advertisement

Post-match, King’s words to his players have summed up his approach perfectly. “I could throw up numbers, but they don’t really matter,” King said. Internally, the same word keeps coming up. Three people we spoke to for this article who wished to remain anonymous to speak freely, were asked what is behind their unexpected rise, they all replied, “fun”. Fun is not a word anyone has attached to Melbourne for a long time, but King – who is said to have a very dry sense of humour – brought a philosophy to celebrate players’ strengths and encourage them to bring them to life through hard work.

Advertisement

He can deliver hard truths when required, and knows the game exceptionally well, having done a true apprenticeship playing football at Geelong and St Kilda under Gary Ayres, Mark Thompson and Ross Lyon (he won a flag with the Cats) before coaching at the Western Bulldogs (where he was involved in the 2016 flag and 2021 grand final), the Gold Coast and then the Cats. He gives his players freedom, instilling belief by referring to their strengths, and has been a popular, respected figure at each of the clubs he served. Melbourne are genuine premiership contenders in 2026 Getty Images King also studied hard, throwing himself into a football manager’s course at the Cats while simultaneously coaching the midfield and sacrificing family time to pursue his ambition. He is off to a good start. One competition source who has watched him evolve said he has taken anxiety out of his players’ minds. Funnily enough, he has done the same to Melbourne supporters who gave him a standing ovation after the win over the Dockers.

Advertisement

The Demons – who built a strong foundation to their game under Simon Goodwin – have now won six of their seven matches since being seventh on the ladder at their bye. Their scores from turnover per game sits second only to Geelong in the past five matches, and they generate scores from their defensive half at a higher percentage than any other team in that time. Only Sydney has generated more scores from centre bounces in the past five games. Their football is exciting, a front-running style, akin to Vo Rogue or Pride of Jenni, which dares other teams to go with them. They are in the top four for scoring, but concede scores, too, sitting 14th for points against. All that has put them fifth on the ladder heading into the final round, having cocooned the football department from potentially destabilising events, such as the departure of the CEO and legal action against the club over what was allegedly said in a meeting called to discuss May’s absence from the group.

During the week they re-signed emerging midfielder Tom Sparrow, who had a mighty offer from Port Adelaide, having retained Kade Chandler, who has built a career through hard work to be recognised in 2026. Related Article Updated

King has led the team into finals in his first season, with wins over Hawthorn, the Brisbane Lions and Fremantle on his resume. Alongside Fremantle’s Justin Longmuir and Carlton’s Josh Fraser he is destroying the myth that ruckmen can’t coach. Ever the optimist, King is not too worried about where they finish.

title: Aussie's $300k gamble as shoppers turn their backs on supermarkets: 'People are craving it'
text:
For Brehoni Renk, the simple belief that Australians should have an easier way to share what they grow in their own backyards sparked an idea.

Six and a half years later, the Perth business owner has poured around $300,000 into turning that idea into reality.

Incaberry is a free app designed to connect people with homegrown produce and, hopefully, with each other.

It comes as frustrated shoppers are increasingly turning their backs on major supermarkets, like Coles and Woolworths.

Do you grow fruits and vegetables in your own garden? Contact

Brehoni Renk has spent $300,000 building a free app designed to connect Australians through homegrown produce. Source: Supplied

'Living in our own little bubbles'

Incaberry allows people to buy, sell and swap homegrown produce, including fruit, vegetables, herbs and flowers, as well as preserves and baked goods.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

But for Brehoni, the bigger idea was never simply creating another online marketplace.

She believes Aussie households have become increasingly disconnected from their neighbours, with many people living in their own "little bubbles".

"We've become used to living in our own little bubbles — going to work, coming home, maybe knowing a few neighbours but not really having much of a connection with them," she said.

Brehoni Renk hopes Incaberry can help Australians reconnect with their neighbours. Source: Supplied

"Social media has made us feel connected without genuinely connecting."

Brehoni believes home growers are an "undersupported community", with many producing more than they need but lacking an easy way to share it.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She hopes Incaberry provides a "permission slip" to connect — whether that means sharing spare lemons or flowers with a neighbour.

"I think that kind of connection has been lost, and a lot of people are craving it," she said.

For Brehoni, the idea was so important that she quickly decided to turn it into a reality.

She said she was content with her life when the idea first came to her, but wanted to create something she could "stand behind 100 per cent".

"I realised I'd found something I could stand behind completely, something that could make a real, positive impact on the world," she said.

The leap from idea to action took just a week.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

After researching whether something similar already existed, Brehoni couldn't find a platform that offered the community connection she had envisioned.

"I knew I was at a crossroads: either commit fully to building it myself, or step back and wait for someone else to," she said.

"I went all in, and once I was committed, there was no going back."

Backyard connections made as diverse produce range offered

Some of the early interactions on Incaberry have shown Brehoni exactly what she hoped the platform could create.

One user told her they had bought "bum nuggets" — eggs — from a neighbour, which made her laugh.

Another user said they had made five connections in their neighbourhood within just a few weeks of using the app.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Brehoni has been excited by the diversity of produce growing nearby, including dragon fruit and medicinal plants.

One new father told her his wife was "literally celebrating" after discovering the app, following her search for local produce for their family.

RELATED

Brehoni said the response has reinforced her belief that Incaberry is creating something people genuinely want, with thousands of Australians now using the app and hundreds making connections through it.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I've always known it was worth it, long before it appeared that way externally," she added.

"Now it's simply about creating that value for more people, helping more people to make these connections feel part of something bigger than themselves, share their produce, and connect over food."

Incaberry is free for growers and buyers, with Brehoni saying the core mission of connecting communities and sharing produce will remain free as the business develops other revenue streams.
